content/chapters/01b-persistence.md::ch:.review_asset_definitions:
# Stable representations can accumulate error {#ch:PERSISTENCE} The next distinction is between a value and the activity that represents it. Eye position is one number, but a circuit can represent it through thousands of neural activities. A disturbance can change those activities without changing the represented value. Another disturbance can leave a coherent activity pattern while changing the value. The geometry of these two changes will explain why a stable-looking circuit can still accumulate memory error.[^f-memory] We first build a small example in which some disturbances fade while others leave a different stored angle. We then ask what happens when small lasting changes arrive repeatedly, deriving how their spread grows with time and how a fixed bias changes that prediction. The final distinction is between this changing value and an irregular spatial map that stays fixed. It explains why the memory, eye-motion, and place-field papers need different models even though all three concern variable neural signals. ## Stable activity with a vulnerable stored value {#sec:FOUNDATIONS-ATTRACTOR} Imagine a group of neurons maintaining a pattern that represents an eye angle after a movement command has ended. Random spikes disturb that pattern. Recurrent input can correct some disturbances by changing the cells' firing back toward a persistent pattern. But if a disturbance produces the pattern for a different angle, an ideal memory circuit has no record of which angle was originally intended. [Keeping a pattern stable is therefore different from keeping the stored value correct.]{.key-statement} [A circuit's current activities are its [**state**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} A dynamical equation specifies how that state changes. [A [**fixed point**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a state where the deterministic rate of change is zero.]{.definition-explanation} It is stable in a direction if a small disturbance in that direction decays. Memory of a continuous quantity calls for a family of persistent states. [A [**continuous attractor**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a continuous family of fixed points with restoring dynamics toward the family and a neutral direction along it. Neutral means that there is no restoring force along that direction in the ideal deterministic model.]{.definition-explanation} [The family is an [**attractor manifold**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Its dimension counts independent coordinates represented on it, rather than neurons in the circuit.]{.definition-explanation} A line attractor has one represented coordinate. A ring can represent a periodic coordinate such as heading.[^f-memory] In the illustrative two-cell model below, the difference between the firing rates represents the angle. Raising both rates equally leaves that difference unchanged. The model's feedback removes the common increase. Raising one rate while lowering the other changes the represented angle. That second change persists. The calculation makes these two responses explicit. It is not a fitted biological circuit.
[**Example: two disturbances to the same stored angle**]{#sec-foundations-attractor-example} Consider a teaching model with two activities $r_1,r_2$ in spikes per second. Let $b=40$ spikes per second and let $k=2$ spikes per second per degree. A stored angle $\theta$ corresponds to $$ r_1=b+k\theta,\qquad r_2=b-k\theta. $$ The fixed points lie on the line $r_1+r_2=2b$. Restrict attention to angles where both rates remain positive. Define the deviation in their mean activity and the represented angle as $$ x=\frac{r_1+r_2}{2}-b, \qquad \theta=\frac{r_1-r_2}{2k}. $$ Suppose each activity changes according to $$ \dot r_1=-a x,\qquad \dot r_2=-a x, $$ where $a>0$ has units inverse seconds. Adding and subtracting these equations gives $$ \dot x=-a x,\qquad \dot\theta=0. $$ The first equation has solution $x(t)=x(0)e^{-at}$, so disturbances in the common activity decay. The second equation retains any angle set by the initial state. Increasing $a$ shortens the recovery time $1/a$ for the common activity disturbance. It does not correct the angle error, because $\dot\theta$ is still zero. At fixed rate disturbance, a larger tuning slope $k$ gives a smaller decoded angle change through division by $2k$. Changing $k$ in an actual circuit may also change its dynamics. At $\theta=5$ degrees, the rates are $(50,30)$. Compare two disturbances from this same state: - A disturbance of $(+3,+3)$ changes the rates to $(53,33)$. It creates $x=3$ but leaves the represented angle at 5 degrees. The restoring dynamics return to $(50,30)$. - A disturbance of $(+3,-3)$ gives $(53,27)$, with $x=0$ and angle $26/(2\times2)=6.5$ degrees. This state lies on the fixed-point line, so there is no restoring response. [In the second case, the circuit remains coherent while holding the wrong angle.]{.key-statement} The two changes occupy different directions in the activity plane. The solid arrow in the figure is the restoring motion produced by the model. The dashed arrow shows the imposed disturbance along the fixed-point line, rather than a deterministic restoring flow. {{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-ATTRACTOR}} In a larger network, the lasting change depends on its connection weights and cannot always be found by an ordinary perpendicular projection. The [network calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization) derives the correct projection from the network's linearized dynamics.
## Independent steps with equal duration and variance give linear variance growth {#sec:FOUNDATIONS-DIFFUSION} Each extra or missing spike changes synaptic input. After the circuit has corrected the disturbances it can remove, a small change in the represented angle may remain. Repeating this process makes trials that began at the same angle gradually spread apart. We first model these lasting changes as independent, with no preferred direction and a constant variance per unit time. These are assumptions about the surviving changes, not about complete spike trains. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Mathematical model: independent steps and Brownian motion"} Divide time into intervals of length $\Delta t$. Let $\xi_j$ be the change in the represented coordinate during interval $j$. The calculation assumes: - Increments are independent. - Each increment has mean zero. - Each increment has variance $2D\Delta t$, where $D$ has units coordinate squared per time. After $n$ intervals, $$ \theta_n-\theta_0=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\xi_j, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\theta_n-\theta_0) =\sum_{j=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(\xi_j) =2Dn\Delta t. $$ Writing $t=n\Delta t$ gives linear variance growth $2Dt$. [To describe this limit with a continuous path, use [**Brownian motion**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $W(t)$. It starts at zero, has continuous paths and independent Gaussian increments with mean zero, and satisfies $\operatorname{Var}[W(t)-W(s)]=t-s$ for $t\geq s$.]{.definition-explanation} It describes the limit of many small, suitably independent fluctuations. A physical network need only approach this description over the time and noise scales relevant to the calculation. In this continuous diffusion approximation, $$ \theta(t)=\theta(0)+\sqrt{2D}\,W(t), \qquad \mathbb E[(\theta(t)-\theta(0))^2]=2Dt. $$ ::: [The **diffusion coefficient** $D$ measures half the rate at which the variance of the stored angle grows.]{.definition-explanation} With independent, zero-mean increments of constant variance per unit time, $$ \operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\theta(0)]=2Dt. $$ Here $D$ has units degrees squared per second when $\theta$ is in degrees. More frequent retained disturbances, or larger ones at the same frequency, increase $D$. At a fixed delay, doubling $D$ doubles error variance and multiplies its standard deviation by $\sqrt{2}$. [A single memory trajectory can turn back even while the spread across trials grows.]{.key-statement} The [network calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion) obtains $D$ from the spike variability and the lasting effect of each cell's disturbance. The mean squared displacement, or MSD, is the expected squared change across a lag. In the zero-mean diffusion just defined, MSD is $2Dt$. [A [**root mean squared displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is its square root, $\sqrt{2Dt}$, and has the same units as the represented coordinate.]{.definition-explanation} In several dimensions, adding independent coordinate contributions gives an overall MSD of $2dDt$ only when each of the $d$ coordinates has the same diffusion coefficient. A paper that defines its diffusion parameter as the entire two-dimensional MSD slope uses a different convention.
[**Example: why the noise grows slower than a fixed bias**]{#sec-foundations-diffusion-example} Take an illustrative angular diffusion coefficient $D=0.02$ degrees squared per second. At 0.35 s its variance is $0.014$ degrees squared and its root mean squared displacement is 0.118 degrees, or about 7.10 arcminutes. At 1 s the root mean squared displacement is 0.20 degrees. If there is also a constant bias velocity $v=0.10$ degrees per second, then $$ \theta(t)-\theta(0)=vt+\sqrt{2D}\,W(t), \qquad \operatorname{MSD}(t)=v^2t^2+2Dt. $$ The deterministic and random contributions are equal at $t=2D/v^2=4$ seconds. Their equal contributions there are each $0.16$ degrees squared. At longer times the bias dominates this unbounded model even though it was small over a short observation. A theory of random diffusion must account separately for [**systematic drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a nonzero mean velocity. Sample paths show the irregular motion. Exact displacement scales show how its spread differs from a fixed bias.
{{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-DIFFUSION-BIAS}}
A constant bias grows linearly, so it eventually exceeds the square root growth of the random displacement scale. See [Gaussian displacement density, SI Eq. S30, p. 7](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=7).
A later memory state contains earlier accumulated errors as well as new ones. Observing it twice therefore does not give two independent copies of the original memory. The covariance calculation below quantifies the shared history used in the readout chapter. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Mathematical detail: why two times share accumulated noise"} Two times along a Brownian path are correlated even though its increments are independent. For $0\leq s\leq t$, write $W(t)=W(s)+[W(t)-W(s)]$. The bracketed increment is independent of $W(s)$ and has mean zero, giving $$ \operatorname{Cov}(W(s),W(t)) =\operatorname{Var}(W(s))=s, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(W(s),W(t))=\min(s,t). $$ The same argument gives covariance $2D\min(s,t)$ for a diffusing coordinate started at a fixed value. This identity is the intermediate step needed to compute the error from averaging a memory that moves during readout. It also helps explain why smoothing a diffusive input is different from smoothing a stationary noise source. ::: A finite range, a periodic coordinate, external feedback, or a position-dependent diffusion coefficient changes long-time behavior. For example, ordinary squared angular distance on a ring cannot keep growing linearly forever. The basic $2Dt$ result is local or unbounded unless those conditions are treated separately. ## A fixed spatial map differs from a value that wanders over time {#sec:FOUNDATIONS-RANDOMNESS} The memory and eye papers study fluctuations that accumulate as time passes. The place-field paper instead starts with a random function of physical position. Once drawn for a cell and an environment, that function is fixed while the animal moves through the map. Revisiting a place evaluates the same expected-rate function, although the actual spikes can still vary from visit to visit. These two kinds of randomness can occur together. A circuit may maintain a position estimate with time-dependent noise, while downstream cells respond to position through irregular but repeatable tuning curves. [Observing irregular spatial maps does not tell us how fast the maintained position drifts. Conversely, finding diffusion of a stored value does not determine the shapes of individual place fields.]{.key-statement} The following chapters develop the dynamical calculation first, then the experiment that tests a possible consequence, and finally the spatial statistics.[^f-place] The three questions can now be placed beside the kind of variation each paper studies.
{{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-PAPER-MAP}}
The rows compare different questions. They do not establish one circuit connecting all three papers. [^f-memory]: Burak, Y., and Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 109(43), 17645–17650. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). Introduction, Fig. 1, and SI I–III. The two-activity example is a guide construction illustrating the geometry, not the paper's simulated network. [^f-place]: Mainali, N., Azeredo da Silveira, R., and Burak, Y. (2025). *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*. Neuron, 113(7), 1110–1120.e3. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017). Introduction, Results, and STAR Methods. The distinction between map randomness and visit-to-visit spike variation follows from what the model's random function indexes.

review_metadata.title: Stable representations can accumulate error
review_metadata.purpose: A neural circuit can sustain its firing while the value represented by that firing changes. Using eye angle as an example, this chapter separates changes in the activity of the cells from changes in the stored value. That distinction explains how persistent activity can still accumulate memory error.

# Stable representations can accumulate error {#ch:PERSISTENCE} The next distinction is between a value and the activity that represents it. Eye position is one number, but a circuit can represent it through thousands of neural activities. A disturbance can change those activities without changing the represented value. We then ask what happens when small lasting changes arrive repeatedly, deriving how their spread grows with time and how a fixed bias changes that prediction. The final distinction is between this changing value and an irregular spatial map that stays fixed. [A [**continuous attractor**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a continuous family of fixed points with restoring dynamics toward the family and a neutral direction along it. Neutral means that there is no restoring force along that direction in the ideal deterministic model.]{.definition-explanation} [The family is an [**attractor manifold**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Its dimension counts independent coordinates represented on it, rather than neurons in the circuit.]{.definition-explanation} A line attractor has one represented coordinate. Define the deviation in their mean activity and the represented angle as $$ x=\frac{r_1+r_2}{2}-b, \qquad \theta=\frac{r_1-r_2}{2k}. $$ Suppose each activity changes according to $$ \dot r_1=-a x,\qquad \dot r_2=-a x, $$ where $a>0$ has units inverse seconds. ## Independent steps with equal duration and variance give linear variance growth {#sec:FOUNDATIONS-DIFFUSION} Each extra or missing spike changes synaptic input. After the circuit has corrected the disturbances it can remove, a small change in the represented angle may remain. Repeating this process makes trials that began at the same angle gradually spread apart. We first model these lasting changes as independent, with no preferred direction and a constant variance per unit time. These are assumptions about the surviving changes, not about complete spike trains. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Mathematical model: independent steps and Brownian motion"} Divide time into intervals of length $\Delta t$. Let $\xi_j$ be the change in the represented coordinate during interval $j$. The calculation assumes: - Increments are independent. - Each increment has mean zero. - Each increment has variance $2D\Delta t$, where $D$ has units coordinate squared per time. After $n$ intervals, $$ \theta_n-\theta_0=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\xi_j, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\theta_n-\theta_0) =\sum_{j=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(\xi_j) =2Dn\Delta t. $$ Writing $t=n\Delta t$ gives linear variance growth $2Dt$. [To describe this limit with a continuous path, use [**Brownian motion**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $W(t)$. It starts at zero, has continuous paths and independent Gaussian increments with mean zero, and satisfies $\operatorname{Var}[W(t)-W(s)]=t-s$ for $t\geq s$.]{.definition-explanation} It describes the limit of many small, suitably independent fluctuations. A physical network need only approach this description over the time and noise scales relevant to the calculation. In this continuous diffusion approximation, $$ \theta(t)=\theta(0)+\sqrt{2D}\,W(t), \qquad \mathbb E[(\theta(t)-\theta(0))^2]=2Dt. $$ ::: [The **diffusion coefficient** $D$ measures half the rate at which the variance of the stored angle grows.]{.definition-explanation} With independent, zero-mean increments of constant variance per unit time, $$ \operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\theta(0)]=2Dt. $$ Here $D$ has units degrees squared per second when $\theta$ is in degrees. More frequent retained disturbances, or larger ones at the same frequency, increase $D$. At a fixed delay, doubling $D$ doubles error variance and multiplies its standard deviation by $\sqrt{2}$. [A single memory trajectory can turn back even while the spread across trials grows.]{.key-statement} The [network calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion) obtains $D$ from the spike variability and the lasting effect of each cell's disturbance. The mean squared displacement, or MSD, is the expected squared change across a lag. In the zero-mean diffusion just defined, MSD is $2Dt$. [A [**root mean squared displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is its square root, $\sqrt{2Dt}$, and has the same units as the represented coordinate.]{.definition-explanation} In several dimensions, adding independent coordinate contributions gives an overall MSD of $2dDt$ only when each of the $d$ coordinates has the same diffusion coefficient. A paper that defines its diffusion parameter as the entire two-dimensional MSD slope uses a different convention.
[**Example: why the noise grows slower than a fixed bias**]{#sec-foundations-diffusion-example} Take an illustrative angular diffusion coefficient $D=0.02$ degrees squared per second. At 0.35 s its variance is $0.014$ degrees squared and its root mean squared displacement is 0.118 degrees, or about 7.10 arcminutes. At 1 s the root mean squared displacement is 0.20 degrees. If there is also a constant bias velocity $v=0.10$ degrees per second, then $$ \theta(t)-\theta(0)=vt+\sqrt{2D}\,W(t), \qquad \operatorname{MSD}(t)=v^2t^2+2Dt. $$ The deterministic and random contributions are equal at $t=2D/v^2=4$ seconds. Their equal contributions there are each $0.16$ degrees squared. At longer times the bias dominates this unbounded model even though it was small over a short observation. A theory of random diffusion must account separately for [**systematic drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a nonzero mean velocity. Sample paths show the irregular motion. Exact displacement scales show how its spread differs from a fixed bias.
{{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-DIFFUSION-BIAS}}
A constant bias grows linearly, so it eventually exceeds the square root growth of the random displacement scale. See [Gaussian displacement density, SI Eq. S30, p. 7](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=7).
A later memory state contains earlier accumulated errors as well as new ones. Observing it twice therefore does not give two independent copies of the original memory. The covariance calculation below quantifies the shared history used in the readout chapter. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Mathematical detail: why two times share accumulated noise"} Two times along a Brownian path are correlated even though its increments are independent. For $0\leq s\leq t$, write $W(t)=W(s)+[W(t)-W(s)]$. The bracketed increment is independent of $W(s)$ and has mean zero, giving $$ \operatorname{Cov}(W(s),W(t)) =\operatorname{Var}(W(s))=s, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(W(s),W(t))=\min(s,t). $$ The same argument gives covariance $2D\min(s,t)$ for a diffusing coordinate started at a fixed value. This identity is the intermediate step needed to compute the error from averaging a memory that moves during readout. It also helps explain why smoothing a diffusive input is different from smoothing a stationary noise source. ::: A finite range, a periodic coordinate, external feedback, or a position-dependent diffusion coefficient changes long-time behavior. For example, ordinary squared angular distance on a ring cannot keep growing linearly forever. The basic $2Dt$ result is local or unbounded unless those conditions are treated separately. ## A fixed spatial map differs from a value that wanders over time {#sec:FOUNDATIONS-RANDOMNESS} The memory and eye papers study fluctuations that accumulate as time passes. The place-field paper instead starts with a random function of physical position. Once drawn for a cell and an environment, that function is fixed while the animal moves through the map. Revisiting a place evaluates the same expected-rate function, although the actual spikes can still vary from visit to visit. These two kinds of randomness can occur together. A circuit may maintain a position estimate with time-dependent noise, while downstream cells respond to position through irregular but repeatable tuning curves. [Observing irregular spatial maps does not tell us how fast the maintained position drifts. Conversely, finding diffusion of a stored value does not determine the shapes of individual place fields.]{.key-statement} The following chapters develop the dynamical calculation first, then the experiment that tests a possible consequence, and finally the spatial statistics.[^f-place] The three questions can now be placed beside the kind of variation each paper studies.
{{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-PAPER-MAP}}
The rows compare different questions. They do not establish one circuit connecting all three papers. [^f-memory]: Burak, Y., and Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 109(43), 17645–17650. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). Introduction, Fig. 1, and SI I–III. The two-activity example is a guide construction illustrating the geometry, not the paper's simulated network. [^f-place]: Mainali, N., Azeredo da Silveira, R., and Burak, Y. (2025). *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*. Neuron, 113(7), 1110–1120.e3. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017). Introduction, Results, and STAR Methods. The distinction between map randomness and visit-to-visit spike variation follows from what the model's random function indexes.

## Independent steps with equal duration and variance give linear variance growth {#sec:FOUNDATIONS-DIFFUSION} Each extra or missing spike changes synaptic input. After the circuit has corrected the disturbances it can remove, a small change in the represented angle may remain. Repeating this process makes trials that began at the same angle gradually spread apart. We first model these lasting changes as independent, with no preferred direction and a constant variance per unit time. These are assumptions about the surviving changes, not about complete spike trains. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Mathematical model: independent steps and Brownian motion"} Divide time into intervals of length $\Delta t$. Let $\xi_j$ be the change in the represented coordinate during interval $j$. The calculation assumes: - Increments are independent. - Each increment has mean zero. - Each increment has variance $2D\Delta t$, where $D$ has units coordinate squared per time. After $n$ intervals, $$ \theta_n-\theta_0=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\xi_j, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\theta_n-\theta_0) =\sum_{j=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(\xi_j) =2Dn\Delta t. $$ Writing $t=n\Delta t$ gives linear variance growth $2Dt$. [To describe this limit with a continuous path, use [**Brownian motion**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $W(t)$. It starts at zero, has continuous paths and independent Gaussian increments with mean zero, and satisfies $\operatorname{Var}[W(t)-W(s)]=t-s$ for $t\geq s$.]{.definition-explanation} It describes the limit of many small, suitably independent fluctuations. A physical network need only approach this description over the time and noise scales relevant to the calculation. In this continuous diffusion approximation, $$ \theta(t)=\theta(0)+\sqrt{2D}\,W(t), \qquad \mathbb E[(\theta(t)-\theta(0))^2]=2Dt. $$ ::: [The **diffusion coefficient** $D$ measures half the rate at which the variance of the stored angle grows.]{.definition-explanation} With independent, zero-mean increments of constant variance per unit time, $$ \operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\theta(0)]=2Dt. $$ Here $D$ has units degrees squared per second when $\theta$ is in degrees. More frequent retained disturbances, or larger ones at the same frequency, increase $D$. At a fixed delay, doubling $D$ doubles error variance and multiplies its standard deviation by $\sqrt{2}$. [A single memory trajectory can turn back even while the spread across trials grows.]{.key-statement} The [network calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion) obtains $D$ from the spike variability and the lasting effect of each cell's disturbance. The mean squared displacement, or MSD, is the expected squared change across a lag. In the zero-mean diffusion just defined, MSD is $2Dt$. [A [**root mean squared displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is its square root, $\sqrt{2Dt}$, and has the same units as the represented coordinate.]{.definition-explanation} In several dimensions, adding independent coordinate contributions gives an overall MSD of $2dDt$ only when each of the $d$ coordinates has the same diffusion coefficient. A paper that defines its diffusion parameter as the entire two-dimensional MSD slope uses a different convention.
[**Example: why the noise grows slower than a fixed bias**]{#sec-foundations-diffusion-example} Take an illustrative angular diffusion coefficient $D=0.02$ degrees squared per second. At 0.35 s its variance is $0.014$ degrees squared and its root mean squared displacement is 0.118 degrees, or about 7.10 arcminutes. At 1 s the root mean squared displacement is 0.20 degrees. If there is also a constant bias velocity $v=0.10$ degrees per second, then $$ \theta(t)-\theta(0)=vt+\sqrt{2D}\,W(t), \qquad \operatorname{MSD}(t)=v^2t^2+2Dt. $$ The deterministic and random contributions are equal at $t=2D/v^2=4$ seconds. Their equal contributions there are each $0.16$ degrees squared. At longer times the bias dominates this unbounded model even though it was small over a short observation. A theory of random diffusion must account separately for [**systematic drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a nonzero mean velocity. Sample paths show the irregular motion. Exact displacement scales show how its spread differs from a fixed bias.
{{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-DIFFUSION-BIAS}}
A constant bias grows linearly, so it eventually exceeds the square root growth of the random displacement scale. See [Gaussian displacement density, SI Eq. S30, p. 7](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=7).
A later memory state contains earlier accumulated errors as well as new ones. Observing it twice therefore does not give two independent copies of the original memory. For $0\leq s\leq t$, write $W(t)=W(s)+[W(t)-W(s)]$. The bracketed increment is independent of $W(s)$ and has mean zero, giving $$ \operatorname{Cov}(W(s),W(t)) =\operatorname{Var}(W(s))=s, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(W(s),W(t))=\min(s,t). $$ The same argument gives covariance $2D\min(s,t)$ for a diffusing coordinate started at a fixed value. review_metadata.title: Stable representations can accumulate error
review_metadata.purpose: A neural circuit can sustain its firing while the value represented by that firing changes. Using eye angle as an example, this chapter separates changes in the activity of the cells from changes in the stored value. That distinction explains how persistent activity can still accumulate memory error.

# Stable representations can accumulate error {#ch:PERSISTENCE} The next distinction is between a value and the activity that represents it. Eye position is one number, but a circuit can represent it through thousands of neural activities. A disturbance can change those activities without changing the represented value. Another disturbance can leave a coherent activity pattern while changing the value. The geometry of these two changes will explain why a stable-looking circuit can still accumulate memory error.[^f-memory] We first build a small example in which some disturbances fade while others leave a different stored angle. We then ask what happens when small lasting changes arrive repeatedly, deriving how their spread grows with time and how a fixed bias changes that prediction. The final distinction is between this changing value and an irregular spatial map that stays fixed. It explains why the memory, eye-motion, and place-field papers need different models even though all three concern variable neural signals. ## Stable activity with a vulnerable stored value {#sec:FOUNDATIONS-ATTRACTOR} Imagine a group of neurons maintaining a pattern that represents an eye angle after a movement command has ended. Random spikes disturb that pattern. Recurrent input can correct some disturbances by changing the cells' firing back toward a persistent pattern. But if a disturbance produces the pattern for a different angle, an ideal memory circuit has no record of which angle was originally intended. [Keeping a pattern stable is therefore different from keeping the stored value correct.]{.key-statement} [A circuit's current activities are its [**state**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} A dynamical equation specifies how that state changes. [A [**fixed point**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a state where the deterministic rate of change is zero.]{.definition-explanation} It is stable in a direction if a small disturbance in that direction decays. Memory of a continuous quantity calls for a family of persistent states. [A [**continuous attractor**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a continuous family of fixed points with restoring dynamics toward the family and a neutral direction along it. Neutral means that there is no restoring force along that direction in the ideal deterministic model.]{.definition-explanation} [The family is an [**attractor manifold**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Its dimension counts independent coordinates represented on it, rather than neurons in the circuit.]{.definition-explanation} A line attractor has one represented coordinate. A ring can represent a periodic coordinate such as heading.[^f-memory] In the illustrative two-cell model below, the difference between the firing rates represents the angle. Raising both rates equally leaves that difference unchanged. The model's feedback removes the common increase. Raising one rate while lowering the other changes the represented angle. That second change persists. The calculation makes these two responses explicit. It is not a fitted biological circuit.
[**Example: two disturbances to the same stored angle**]{#sec-foundations-attractor-example} Consider a teaching model with two activities $r_1,r_2$ in spikes per second. Let $b=40$ spikes per second and let $k=2$ spikes per second per degree. A stored angle $\theta$ corresponds to $$ r_1=b+k\theta,\qquad r_2=b-k\theta. $$ The fixed points lie on the line $r_1+r_2=2b$. Restrict attention to angles where both rates remain positive. Define the deviation in their mean activity and the represented angle as $$ x=\frac{r_1+r_2}{2}-b, \qquad \theta=\frac{r_1-r_2}{2k}. $$ Suppose each activity changes according to $$ \dot r_1=-a x,\qquad \dot r_2=-a x, $$ where $a>0$ has units inverse seconds. Adding and subtracting these equations gives $$ \dot x=-a x,\qquad \dot\theta=0. $$ The first equation has solution $x(t)=x(0)e^{-at}$, so disturbances in the common activity decay. The second equation retains any angle set by the initial state. Increasing $a$ shortens the recovery time $1/a$ for the common activity disturbance. It does not correct the angle error, because $\dot\theta$ is still zero. At fixed rate disturbance, a larger tuning slope $k$ gives a smaller decoded angle change through division by $2k$. Changing $k$ in an actual circuit may also change its dynamics. At $\theta=5$ degrees, the rates are $(50,30)$. Compare two disturbances from this same state: - A disturbance of $(+3,+3)$ changes the rates to $(53,33)$. It creates $x=3$ but leaves the represented angle at 5 degrees. The restoring dynamics return to $(50,30)$. - A disturbance of $(+3,-3)$ gives $(53,27)$, with $x=0$ and angle $26/(2\times2)=6.5$ degrees. This state lies on the fixed-point line, so there is no restoring response. [In the second case, the circuit remains coherent while holding the wrong angle.]{.key-statement} The two changes occupy different directions in the activity plane. The solid arrow in the figure is the restoring motion produced by the model. The dashed arrow shows the imposed disturbance along the fixed-point line, rather than a deterministic restoring flow. {{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-ATTRACTOR}} In a larger network, the lasting change depends on its connection weights and cannot always be found by an ordinary perpendicular projection. The [network calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization) derives the correct projection from the network's linearized dynamics.

review_metadata.title: Stable representations can accumulate error
review_metadata.purpose: A neural circuit can sustain its firing while the value represented by that firing changes. That distinction explains how persistent activity can still accumulate memory error.

# Stable representations can accumulate error {#ch:PERSISTENCE} The next distinction is between a value and the activity that represents it. Eye position is one number, but a circuit can represent it through thousands of neural activities. A disturbance can change those activities without changing the represented value. Another disturbance can leave a coherent activity pattern while changing the value. The geometry of these two changes will explain why a stable-looking circuit can still accumulate memory error.[^f-memory] We first build a small example in which some disturbances fade while others leave a different stored angle. We then ask what happens when small lasting changes arrive repeatedly, deriving how their spread grows with time and how a fixed bias changes that prediction. The final distinction is between this changing value and an irregular spatial map that stays fixed. It explains why the memory, eye-motion, and place-field papers need different models even though all three concern variable neural signals. ## Stable activity with a vulnerable stored value {#sec:FOUNDATIONS-ATTRACTOR} Imagine a group of neurons maintaining a pattern that represents an eye angle after a movement command has ended. Random spikes disturb that pattern. Recurrent input can correct some disturbances by changing the cells' firing back toward a persistent pattern. But if a disturbance produces the pattern for a different angle, an ideal memory circuit has no record of which angle was originally intended. [Keeping a pattern stable is therefore different from keeping the stored value correct.]{.key-statement} [A circuit's current activities are its [**state**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} A dynamical equation specifies how that state changes. [A [**fixed point**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a state where the deterministic rate of change is zero.]{.definition-explanation} It is stable in a direction if a small disturbance in that direction decays. Memory of a continuous quantity calls for a family of persistent states. [A [**continuous attractor**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a continuous family of fixed points with restoring dynamics toward the family and a neutral direction along it. Neutral means that there is no restoring force along that direction in the ideal deterministic model.]{.definition-explanation} [The family is an [**attractor manifold**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Its dimension counts independent coordinates represented on it, rather than neurons in the circuit.]{.definition-explanation} A line attractor has one represented coordinate. A ring can represent a periodic coordinate such as heading.[^f-memory] In the illustrative two-cell model below, the difference between the firing rates represents the angle. Raising both rates equally leaves that difference unchanged. The model's feedback removes the common increase. Raising one rate while lowering the other changes the represented angle. That second change persists. The calculation makes these two responses explicit. It is not a fitted biological circuit.
[**Example: two disturbances to the same stored angle**]{#sec-foundations-attractor-example} Consider a teaching model with two activities $r_1,r_2$ in spikes per second. Let $b=40$ spikes per second and let $k=2$ spikes per second per degree. A stored angle $\theta$ corresponds to $$ r_1=b+k\theta,\qquad r_2=b-k\theta. $$ The fixed points lie on the line $r_1+r_2=2b$. Restrict attention to angles where both rates remain positive. Define the deviation in their mean activity and the represented angle as $$ x=\frac{r_1+r_2}{2}-b, \qquad \theta=\frac{r_1-r_2}{2k}. $$ Suppose each activity changes according to $$ \dot r_1=-a x,\qquad \dot r_2=-a x, $$ where $a>0$ has units inverse seconds. Adding and subtracting these equations gives $$ \dot x=-a x,\qquad \dot\theta=0. $$ The first equation has solution $x(t)=x(0)e^{-at}$, so disturbances in the common activity decay. The second equation retains any angle set by the initial state. Increasing $a$ shortens the recovery time $1/a$ for the common activity disturbance. It does not correct the angle error, because $\dot\theta$ is still zero. At fixed rate disturbance, a larger tuning slope $k$ gives a smaller decoded angle change through division by $2k$. Changing $k$ in an actual circuit may also change its dynamics. At $\theta=5$ degrees, the rates are $(50,30)$. Compare two disturbances from this same state: - A disturbance of $(+3,+3)$ changes the rates to $(53,33)$. It creates $x=3$ but leaves the represented angle at 5 degrees. The restoring dynamics return to $(50,30)$. - A disturbance of $(+3,-3)$ gives $(53,27)$, with $x=0$ and angle $26/(2\times2)=6.5$ degrees. This state lies on the fixed-point line, so there is no restoring response. [In the second case, the circuit remains coherent while holding the wrong angle.]{.key-statement} The two changes occupy different directions in the activity plane. The solid arrow in the figure is the restoring motion produced by the model. The dashed arrow shows the imposed disturbance along the fixed-point line, rather than a deterministic restoring flow. {{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-ATTRACTOR}} In a larger network, the lasting change depends on its connection weights and cannot always be found by an ordinary perpendicular projection. The [network calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization) derives the correct projection from the network's linearized dynamics.
## Independent steps with equal duration and variance give linear variance growth {#sec:FOUNDATIONS-DIFFUSION} Each extra or missing spike changes synaptic input. After the circuit has corrected the disturbances it can remove, a small change in the represented angle may remain. Repeating this process makes trials that began at the same angle gradually spread apart. We first model these lasting changes as independent, with no preferred direction and a constant variance per unit time. These are assumptions about the surviving changes, not about complete spike trains. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Mathematical model: independent steps and Brownian motion"} Divide time into intervals of length $\Delta t$. Let $\xi_j$ be the change in the represented coordinate during interval $j$. The calculation assumes: - Increments are independent. - Each increment has mean zero. - Each increment has variance $2D\Delta t$, where $D$ has units coordinate squared per time. After $n$ intervals, $$ \theta_n-\theta_0=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\xi_j, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\theta_n-\theta_0) =\sum_{j=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(\xi_j) =2Dn\Delta t. $$ Writing $t=n\Delta t$ gives linear variance growth $2Dt$. [To describe this limit with a continuous path, use [**Brownian motion**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $W(t)$. It starts at zero, has continuous paths and independent Gaussian increments with mean zero, and satisfies $\operatorname{Var}[W(t)-W(s)]=t-s$ for $t\geq s$.]{.definition-explanation} It describes the limit of many small, suitably independent fluctuations. A physical network need only approach this description over the time and noise scales relevant to the calculation. In this continuous diffusion approximation, $$ \theta(t)=\theta(0)+\sqrt{2D}\,W(t), \qquad \mathbb E[(\theta(t)-\theta(0))^2]=2Dt. $$ ::: [The **diffusion coefficient** $D$ measures half the rate at which the variance of the stored angle grows.]{.definition-explanation} With independent, zero-mean increments of constant variance per unit time, $$ \operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\theta(0)]=2Dt. $$ Here $D$ has units degrees squared per second when $\theta$ is in degrees. More frequent retained disturbances, or larger ones at the same frequency, increase $D$. At a fixed delay, doubling $D$ doubles error variance and multiplies its standard deviation by $\sqrt{2}$. [A single memory trajectory can turn back even while the spread across trials grows.]{.key-statement} The [network calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion) obtains $D$ from the spike variability and the lasting effect of each cell's disturbance. The mean squared displacement, or MSD, is the expected squared change across a lag. In the zero-mean diffusion just defined, MSD is $2Dt$. [A [**root mean squared displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is its square root, $\sqrt{2Dt}$, and has the same units as the represented coordinate.]{.definition-explanation} In several dimensions, adding independent coordinate contributions gives an overall MSD of $2dDt$ only when each of the $d$ coordinates has the same diffusion coefficient. A paper that defines its diffusion parameter as the entire two-dimensional MSD slope uses a different convention.
[**Example: why the noise grows slower than a fixed bias**]{#sec-foundations-diffusion-example} Take an illustrative angular diffusion coefficient $D=0.02$ degrees squared per second. At 0.35 s its variance is $0.014$ degrees squared and its root mean squared displacement is 0.118 degrees, or about 7.10 arcminutes. At 1 s the root mean squared displacement is 0.20 degrees. If there is also a constant bias velocity $v=0.10$ degrees per second, then $$ \theta(t)-\theta(0)=vt+\sqrt{2D}\,W(t), \qquad \operatorname{MSD}(t)=v^2t^2+2Dt. $$ The deterministic and random contributions are equal at $t=2D/v^2=4$ seconds. Their equal contributions there are each $0.16$ degrees squared. At longer times the bias dominates this unbounded model even though it was small over a short observation. A theory of random diffusion must account separately for [**systematic drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a nonzero mean velocity. Sample paths show the irregular motion. Exact displacement scales show how its spread differs from a fixed bias.
{{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-DIFFUSION-BIAS}}
A constant bias grows linearly, so it eventually exceeds the square root growth of the random displacement scale. See [Gaussian displacement density, SI Eq. S30, p. 7](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=7).
A later memory state contains earlier accumulated errors as well as new ones. Observing it twice therefore does not give two independent copies of the original memory. The covariance calculation below quantifies the shared history used in the readout chapter. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Mathematical detail: why two times share accumulated noise"} Two times along a Brownian path are correlated even though its increments are independent. For $0\leq s\leq t$, write $W(t)=W(s)+[W(t)-W(s)]$. The bracketed increment is independent of $W(s)$ and has mean zero, giving $$ \operatorname{Cov}(W(s),W(t)) =\operatorname{Var}(W(s))=s, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(W(s),W(t))=\min(s,t). $$ The same argument gives covariance $2D\min(s,t)$ for a diffusing coordinate started at a fixed value. This identity is the intermediate step needed to compute the error from averaging a memory that moves during readout. It also helps explain why smoothing a diffusive input is different from smoothing a stationary noise source. ::: A finite range, a periodic coordinate, external feedback, or a position-dependent diffusion coefficient changes long-time behavior. For example, ordinary squared angular distance on a ring cannot keep growing linearly forever. The basic $2Dt$ result is local or unbounded unless those conditions are treated separately. ## A fixed spatial map differs from a value that wanders over time {#sec:FOUNDATIONS-RANDOMNESS} The memory and eye papers study fluctuations that accumulate as time passes. The place-field paper instead starts with a random function of physical position. Once drawn for a cell and an environment, that function is fixed while the animal moves through the map. Revisiting a place evaluates the same expected-rate function, although the actual spikes can still vary from visit to visit. These two kinds of randomness can occur together. A circuit may maintain a position estimate with time-dependent noise, while downstream cells respond to position through irregular but repeatable tuning curves. [Observing irregular spatial maps does not tell us how fast the maintained position drifts. Conversely, finding diffusion of a stored value does not determine the shapes of individual place fields.]{.key-statement} The following chapters develop the dynamical calculation first, then the experiment that tests a possible consequence, and finally the spatial statistics.[^f-place] The three questions can now be placed beside the kind of variation each paper studies.
{{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-PAPER-MAP}}
The rows compare different questions. They do not establish one circuit connecting all three papers. [^f-memory]: Burak, Y., and Fiete, I. R. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). Introduction, Fig. 1, and SI I–III. The two-activity example is a guide construction illustrating the geometry, not the paper's simulated network. [^f-place]: Mainali, N., Azeredo da Silveira, R., and Burak, Y. (2025). *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*. Neuron, 113(7), 1110–1120.e3. To calculate the loss of accuracy, we first describe how spikes renew synaptic activity as it decays. Adding these lasting random changes gives a local rate of spreading. When connections have equal weights in both directions, we can express that rate using the cells' tuning curves and check its meaning in a two-cell example. # Spiking noise produces diffusion along the memory attractor {#ch:MEMORY-DYNAMICS}

[A network can keep firing after a stimulus disappears and still lose the value that the stimulus supplied.]{.key-statement} Burak and Fiete study this distinction in a network whose stable activity patterns form a continuous set.[^p1-model]

To calculate the loss of accuracy, we first describe how spikes renew synaptic activity as it decays. We then follow a small disturbance through the circuit's return toward a stable pattern and identify the change in stored value that remains. Adding these lasting random changes gives a local rate of spreading. When connections have equal weights in both directions, we can express that rate using the cells' tuning curves and check its meaning in a two-cell example. The following chapter extends this local prediction to longer delays.

review_metadata.title: Spiking noise produces diffusion along the memory attractor
review_metadata.purpose: Burak and Fiete model a group of interacting neurons that retains a continuous value after an input ends. This chapter follows spikes through their effects at synapses and back into firing, then derives how random spike timing displaces the stored value.

section_list.title: Recurrent spikes renew decaying synaptic activity
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** How can brief spikes maintain a state for much longer than the duration of a spike? In this model, each spike leaves a synaptic activation that decays gradually. Incoming activations determine new firing rates. The resulting spikes renew those activations. This feedback can support activity after the external stimulus has ended.

section_list.title: The network's return flow determines the lasting memory change
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** A spike perturbs many aspects of a network's state. Most of those changes decay as the state returns to the attractor. To calculate memory loss, we need the lasting change: the displacement to a different fixed point. We assume a smooth continuous family with one neutral memory direction, while all other local modes decay. The disturbance must be small enough that the first order response describes the return flow.

section_list.title: Projecting spike fluctuations gives the diffusion coefficient
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** We can now calculate how much random displacement remains after the stable components have relaxed. Each cell's random spikes disturb its outgoing synaptic activation. The circuit's return flow determines the lasting shift in memory. This calculation uses the weak noise and conditional independence assumptions, with rates and return flow evaluated near one fixed point.

section_list.title: Symmetric weights express diffusion through tuning curves
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** The general formula requires the left vector of the network dynamics. When $W_{ij}=W_{ji}$, can we express it through the tuning curves and neural transfer function? Symmetric connections make each cell affect another cell's input with the same weight that it receives in return, while their firing responses can still differ. We retain the common synaptic time constant, a stable continuous family, and the weak noise and conditional independence assumptions.

A one dimensional diffusion coefficient $D$ has units of memory coordinate squared per time, with the convention $\operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\Theta]=2Dt$ when $D$ is constant and boundaries do not matter. ## Recurrent spikes renew decaying synaptic activity {#sec:MEMORY-SPIKES} **Neural mechanism.** How can brief spikes maintain a state for much longer than the duration of a spike? The connections are tuned to a continuous family of steady patterns. The Gaussian description below also assumes weak fluctuations in total input. **Mathematical derivation.** To combine discrete events with continuous decay, a count process records the events and a decay equation records how their effects fade. Here $N_i(t)$ counts neuron $i$'s spikes up to time $t$. The activation $s_i$ tracks the decaying synaptic effect of those outgoing spikes on receiving cells. It rises by one at each spike and otherwise decays: $$ ds_i=-\frac{s_i}{\tau}\,dt+dN_i(t). $$ Equivalently, if its spikes occur at times $t_i^\alpha$, $$ s_i(t)=\sum_{t_i^\alpha {{block:fig:MEMORY-SPIKE-TRACE}} The activation retains a decaying contribution from earlier spikes, so a spike train and its activation trace are different objects. The rate $r_i$ has units of spikes per second. The summed input and the firing rule are $$ g_i=\sum_j W_{ij}s_j+b_i, \qquad r_i=\phi(g_i). $$ The fixed weights $W_{ij}$ say how neuron $j$ affects neuron $i$, and $b_i$ is a constant input. [The [**neural transfer function**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $\phi$ converts total input into a nonnegative firing rate.]{.definition-explanation} For example, increasing input might increase firing linearly over some input range, or exponentially. The paper allows general connectivity and transfer functions at first ([Model, Eqs. 7–9, p. 5](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=5&zoom=125,0,372)).[^p1-model] A spike from cell $j$ raises $s_j$ by one and therefore changes the input to cell $i$ by $W_{ij}$. That contribution then decays over time $\tau$. For an increasing transfer function, a positive weight raises the receiving cell's rate and a negative weight lowers it. The resulting new spikes affect other cells in turn. Thus the weights set where a disturbance goes, the transfer function sets the rate response, and $\tau$ sets how long each synaptic contribution lasts. The input $g_i$ is in the model's input units. It is not specified as a measured membrane voltage. Conditioned on the present rates, spike counts over a short interval $dt$ are independent Poisson variables. Thus $$ E[dN_i\mid r_i]=r_i\,dt, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(dN_i,dN_j\mid\mathbf r) =\delta_{ij}r_i\,dt. $$ The symbol $\delta_{ij}$ is one when $i=j$ and zero otherwise. Splitting the count into its mean and fluctuation gives $$ ds_i=\left[-\frac{s_i}{\tau}+\phi(g_i)\right]dt+dM_i, \qquad E[dM_i]=0, \quad E[dM_i dM_j]=\delta_{ij}r_i\,dt. $$ This is still a jump process. [In the paper's [**weak fluctuation approximation**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, many individually small spike contributions produce only small changes in each neuron's total input. Their summed fluctuation can then be represented by Gaussian noise with the same leading mean and covariance:]{.definition-explanation} $$ ds_i=F_i(\mathbf s)dt+\sqrt{r_i}\,dB_i, \qquad F_i(\mathbf s)=-s_i/\tau+\phi\!\left(\sum_jW_{ij}s_j+b_i\right), $$ where the $B_i$ are independent standard Brownian processes. The noise coefficient has units $\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}$, so its product with $dB_i$ is a dimensionless activation increment. The Gaussian approximation is for small fluctuations in total input. It does not require each single neuron's entire spike train to look like a Gaussian process ([SI Eqs. S2–S5, p. 2](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=2&zoom=125,0,128)).[^p1-weak] The supplement makes this limit concrete by replacing each population with $n$ equivalent neurons and dividing each connection weight by $n$. A summed input has a mean proportional to $n/n=1$, while its variance is proportional to $n/n^2=1/n$. Increasing population size therefore keeps the mean dynamics fixed and reduces input fluctuations. [For a ring network, a neuron's [**preferred angle**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is an angle where its tuning curve peaks.]{.definition-explanation} Increasing the density of equally spaced preferred angles and scaling weights as $1/N$ serves the same purpose. The paper's formulas give the leading terms in this large population limit, rather than exact finite network identities.[^p1-large] Setting noise to zero gives the deterministic rate dynamics $\dot{\mathbf s}=\mathbf F(\mathbf s)$. A continuous attractor is a family of fixed points satisfying $$ 0=-\frac{\bar s_i(\theta)}{\tau} +\phi[\bar g_i(\theta)], \qquad \bar s_i(\theta)=\tau\bar r_i(\theta). $$ **Interpretation.** In the noise free dynamics, recurrent firing balances synaptic decay at each fixed point. The network must be tuned to possess this family. An arbitrary recurrent network will generally have isolated fixed points rather than a whole line or ring of them. ## The network's return flow determines the lasting memory change {#sec:MEMORY-LINEARIZATION} **Neural mechanism.** A spike perturbs many aspects of a network's state. Most of those changes decay as the state returns to the attractor. [To calculate memory loss, we need the lasting change: the displacement to a different fixed point. We assume a smooth continuous family with one neutral memory direction, while all other local modes decay. The disturbance must be small enough that the first order response describes the return flow.]{.key-statement} **Mathematical derivation.** [A [**linearization**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} keeps the terms proportional to a small perturbation and drops terms quadratic or higher in it.]{.definition-explanation} Here the network activation is $\mathbf s=\bar{\mathbf s}(\theta)+\delta\mathbf s$. Taylor expansion of the transfer function gives $$ \phi\!\left(\bar g_i+\sum_j W_{ij}\delta s_j\right) \simeq\phi(\bar g_i)+\phi'(\bar g_i)\sum_jW_{ij}\delta s_j. $$ The constant terms cancel because $\bar{\mathbf s}$ is a fixed point. Therefore $$ d\delta\mathbf s=K\delta\mathbf s\,dt+R^{1/2}d\mathbf B, \qquad K_{ij}=-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\tau}+\phi'(\bar g_i)W_{ij}, \qquad R=\operatorname{diag}(\bar r_i). $$ In this leading local calculation the noise strengths are evaluated at the fixed point. The entries of $K$ have units of inverse time.[^p1-projection] The term $-\delta_{ij}/\tau$ removes a disturbance as synaptic activation fades. The term $\phi'(\bar g_i)W_{ij}$ describes recurrent renewal: the connection converts a change in cell $j$'s activation into input to cell $i$, and the local slope of the transfer function converts that input into a rate change. A steeper slope makes this response stronger. [Whether a disturbance decays, persists, or grows depends on the combined feedback through the whole network.]{.key-statement} A stronger connection alone does not establish better memory. Moving a little along the fixed point family changes the activation by $$ \delta\mathbf s\simeq\mathbf u\,\delta\theta, \qquad u_i=\frac{d\bar s_i}{d\theta}=\tau\frac{d\bar r_i}{d\theta}. $$ Differentiate the fixed point equation $\mathbf F[\bar{\mathbf s}(\theta)]=0$. The chain rule gives $$ K\mathbf u=0. $$ [Thus $\mathbf u$ is a [**right zero eigenvector**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: a state direction that the linear dynamics neither restores nor amplifies.]{.definition-explanation} It is the tangent to the attractor. The other modes must decay for this local family to be attracting. [We also need a [**left zero eigenvector**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a vector $\mathbf v$ satisfying]{.definition-explanation} $$ \mathbf v^T K=0, \qquad \mathbf v^T\mathbf u=1. $$ Its purpose is to extract the lasting memory displacement from a general perturbation. The normalization makes $\mathbf v^T(\mathbf u\,\delta\theta)=\delta\theta$. If a stable mode $\mathbf z$ satisfies $K\mathbf z=\lambda\mathbf z$ with $\lambda\ne0$, then $$ 0=\mathbf v^T K\mathbf z=\lambda\mathbf v^T\mathbf z, $$ so $\mathbf v^T\mathbf z=0$. The left vector discards every decaying mode ([SI Eqs. S12–S13, p. 3](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=3&zoom=125,0,409)). Consequently the surviving part of a small perturbation is $$ \delta\mathbf s_{\mathrm{surviving}} =\mathbf u\,(\mathbf v^T\delta\mathbf s). $$ **Interpretation.** This generally differs from a perpendicular geometric projection. Decay can be tilted relative to the tangent. Even symmetric synaptic weights do not usually make $K$ symmetric, because $\phi'(\bar g_i)$ multiplies different rows by different amounts.
**Example: a disturbance that slides while it decays.** To see the distinction without a neural simulation, consider the local system $$ \dot x=ay,\qquad \dot y=-\lambda y,\quad\lambda>0. $$ Every point with $y=0$ is fixed. Starting from $(x_0,y_0)$ gives $y(t)=y_0e^{-\lambda t}$ and $$ x(\infty)=x_0+\frac{a}{\lambda}y_0. $$ Here $\mathbf u=(1,0)^T$ and $\mathbf v=(1,a/\lambda)^T$. A vertical perturbation changes the final memory whenever $a\ne0$. A perpendicular projection would miss that change. This is a teaching example of the projection geometry, not an additional network used in the paper.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-TILTED-DECAY}}
As $y$ decays, $x$ changes by one. The left vector extracts that lasting shift.
## Projecting spike fluctuations gives the diffusion coefficient {#sec:MEMORY-DIFFUSION} **Neural mechanism.** We can now calculate how much random displacement remains after the stable components have relaxed. [Each cell's random spikes disturb its outgoing synaptic activation. The circuit's return flow determines the lasting shift in memory.]{.key-statement} This calculation uses the weak noise and conditional independence assumptions, with rates and return flow evaluated near one fixed point. **Mathematical derivation.** The variance of a linear combination of independent noise increments is the sum of their variances multiplied by squared weights. Here the weights are the components of $\mathbf v$: multiply the linear stochastic equation by $\mathbf v^T$. Since $\mathbf v^TK=0$, $$ d\theta=\mathbf v^T R^{1/2}d\mathbf B =\sum_i v_i\sqrt{\bar r_i}\,dB_i. $$ The independent Brownian increments have covariance $E[dB_i dB_j]=\delta_{ij}dt$, so $$ E[(d\theta)^2] =\sum_{ij}v_iv_j\sqrt{\bar r_i\bar r_j}\,E[dB_i dB_j] =\left(\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i\right)dt. $$ Matching this to $2D\,dt$ yields the general local result ([SI Eqs. S14–S15, p. 3](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=3&zoom=125,0,576)) $$ \boxed{2D(\theta)=\sum_i v_i(\theta)^2\bar r_i(\theta).} $$ For several memory coordinates $\theta_\alpha$, choose tangent vectors $u_i^\alpha=\partial\bar s_i/\partial\theta_\alpha$ and left vectors with $\sum_i v_i^\alpha u_i^\beta=\delta_{\alpha\beta}$. The same covariance calculation gives $$ 2D_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_i v_i^\alpha\bar r_i v_i^\beta. $$ **Interpretation.** For one memory coordinate, each neuron's contribution combines its spike variability, $\bar r_i$, with the squared effect of one activation fluctuation on the final memory, $v_i^2$. The formula does not say that neurons with high rates necessarily damage memory more: changing rates can also change the tuning curves and the projection weights. Those changes must be included in a comparison.[^p1-projection] The result is local in state and leading order in weak noise. The time interval must satisfy two conditions: - It must be long enough for the approximation based on many spike contributions to apply. - It must be short enough that the coefficients do not change substantially as the memory moves. These conditions justify a local spreading rate. Systematic drift requires a [separate check in the next chapter](ch-memory-long-delays.html#sec-memory-drift-scope). [The [**diffusion tensor**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the matrix of displacement covariances per twice the elapsed time.]{.definition-explanation} Its diagonal entries describe spreading in individual coordinates. Its other entries describe how coordinate displacements vary together. Even independently generated spike-count fluctuations can generate coupled motion of the represented coordinates.[^p1-multid] ## Symmetric weights express diffusion through tuning curves {#sec:MEMORY-SYMMETRIC} **Neural mechanism.** The general formula requires the left vector of the network dynamics. [When $W_{ij}=W_{ji}$, can we express it through the tuning curves and neural transfer function?]{.key-statement} Symmetric connections make each cell affect another cell's input with the same weight that it receives in return, while their firing responses can still differ. We retain the common synaptic time constant, a stable continuous family, and the weak noise and conditional independence assumptions. **Mathematical derivation.** The chain rule relates the slope of a response curve to the slope of its input curve. Here let $g_i'=d\bar g_i/d\theta$ and $r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta$. Differentiating the fixed point identities gives $$ r_i'=\phi'(\bar g_i)g_i', \qquad \mathbf g'=\tau W\mathbf r'. $$ With symmetric $W$, the transpose of the linearized matrix satisfies $$ K^T\mathbf g' =-\mathbf g'/\tau+W\operatorname{diag}[\phi'(\bar g_i)]\mathbf g' =-\mathbf g'/\tau+W\mathbf r'=0. $$ Therefore $\mathbf v$ is proportional to $\mathbf g'$. Its normalization is $$ v_i=\frac{g_i'}{\tau\sum_jr_j'g_j'}, $$ because $u_i=\tau r_i'$. Substituting into the noise projection gives $$ \boxed{ 2D(\theta)= \frac{\sum_i\bar r_i(g_i')^2} {\tau^2[\sum_i r_i'g_i']^2}. } $$ **Interpretation.** The input slopes $g_i'$ now determine the projection weights, so the diffusion coefficient can be calculated from the tuning curves and transfer function. This follows from [SI Eq. S18, p. 4](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=4&zoom=125,0,239), with $\bar g_i=\phi^{-1}(\bar r_i)$ wherever the transfer function is invertible over the relevant range. The supplied Early Edition [main Eq. 2, p. 2](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=2&zoom=125,0,88) appears to omit the square on $g_i'$ in the numerator. The projection calculation and SI S18 give the squared expression shown here. This is an independent source check, not an author-confirmed correction. The result requires: - Symmetric weights. - A stable continuous family. - The noise assumptions already introduced. The result does not require [**translation symmetry**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, in which shifting an activity pattern along the represented coordinate leaves the network dynamics unchanged in form.[^p1-symmetric]
**Example: opposite firing changes with constant diffusion.** Take two mutually inhibiting cells with $W_{12}=W_{21}=-1$, zero self weights, equal biases $b$, and $\phi(g)=g/\tau$ over the positive input range. Its fixed points obey $$ \bar s_1=\frac{b+\theta}{2},\qquad \bar s_2=\frac{b-\theta}{2},\qquad |\theta| Although the two firing rates change with the stored value, their summed spike variability is constant. Therefore this network has constant local diffusion throughout its valid range. Near an endpoint, a negative linear rate would be impossible. A physical implementation must alter the transfer rule, and the interior formula alone does not describe that boundary. This model underlies the mutual inhibition example in [Fig. 2E–G, p. 3](ch-memory-long-delays.html#fig-paper-memory-2).[^p1-two] The plot uses $b=20$ activation units and $\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-INHIBITION-RATES}}
The dashed rate sum in the upper plot stays fixed, so the lower plot has the same $D$ at every interior value of $\theta$.

That contribution then decays over time $\tau$. For an increasing transfer function, a positive weight raises the receiving cell's rate and a negative weight lowers it. The resulting new spikes affect other cells in turn. Thus the weights set where a disturbance goes, the transfer function sets the rate response, and $\tau$ sets how long each synaptic contribution lasts. The input $g_i$ is in the model's input units. It is not specified as a measured membrane voltage. Conditioned on the present rates, spike counts over a short interval $dt$ are independent Poisson variables. Thus $$ E[dN_i\mid r_i]=r_i\,dt, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(dN_i,dN_j\mid\mathbf r) =\delta_{ij}r_i\,dt. $$ The symbol $\delta_{ij}$ is one when $i=j$ and zero otherwise. Splitting the count into its mean and fluctuation gives $$ ds_i=\left[-\frac{s_i}{\tau}+\phi(g_i)\right]dt+dM_i, \qquad E[dM_i]=0, \quad E[dM_i dM_j]=\delta_{ij}r_i\,dt. $$ This is still a jump process. [In the paper's [**weak fluctuation approximation**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, many individually small spike contributions produce only small changes in each neuron's total input. Their summed fluctuation can then be represented by Gaussian noise with the same leading mean and covariance:]{.definition-explanation} $$ ds_i=F_i(\mathbf s)dt+\sqrt{r_i}\,dB_i, \qquad F_i(\mathbf s)=-s_i/\tau+\phi\!\left(\sum_jW_{ij}s_j+b_i\right), $$ where the $B_i$ are independent standard Brownian processes. The noise coefficient has units $\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}$, so its product with $dB_i$ is a dimensionless activation increment. The Gaussian approximation is for small fluctuations in total input. It does not require each single neuron's entire spike train to look like a Gaussian process ([SI Eqs. S2–S5, p. 2](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=2&zoom=125,0,128)).[^p1-weak] The supplement makes this limit concrete by replacing each population with $n$ equivalent neurons and dividing each connection weight by $n$. A summed input has a mean proportional to $n/n=1$, while its variance is proportional to $n/n^2=1/n$. Increasing population size therefore keeps the mean dynamics fixed and reduces input fluctuations. [For a ring network, a neuron's [**preferred angle**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is an angle where its tuning curve peaks.]{.definition-explanation} Increasing the density of equally spaced preferred angles and scaling weights as $1/N$ serves the same purpose. The paper's formulas give the leading terms in this large population limit, rather than exact finite network identities.[^p1-large] Setting noise to zero gives the deterministic rate dynamics $\dot{\mathbf s}=\mathbf F(\mathbf s)$. A continuous attractor is a family of fixed points satisfying $$ 0=-\frac{\bar s_i(\theta)}{\tau} +\phi[\bar g_i(\theta)], \qquad \bar s_i(\theta)=\tau\bar r_i(\theta). $$ **Interpretation.** In the noise free dynamics, recurrent firing balances synaptic decay at each fixed point. The network must be tuned to possess this family. An arbitrary recurrent network will generally have isolated fixed points rather than a whole line or ring of them.

review_metadata.title: Spiking noise produces diffusion along the memory attractor
review_metadata.purpose: Burak and Fiete model a group of interacting neurons that retains a continuous value after an input ends. This chapter follows spikes through their effects at synapses and back into firing, then derives how random spike timing displaces the stored value.

section_list.title: Recurrent spikes renew decaying synaptic activity
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** How can brief spikes maintain a state for much longer than the duration of a spike? In this model, each spike leaves a synaptic activation that decays gradually. Incoming activations determine new firing rates. The resulting spikes renew those activations. This feedback can support activity after the external stimulus has ended.

section_list.title: The network's return flow determines the lasting memory change
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** A spike perturbs many aspects of a network's state. Most of those changes decay as the state returns to the attractor. To calculate memory loss, we need the lasting change: the displacement to a different fixed point. We assume a smooth continuous family with one neutral memory direction, while all other local modes decay. The disturbance must be small enough that the first order response describes the return flow.

section_list.title: Projecting spike fluctuations gives the diffusion coefficient
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** We can now calculate how much random displacement remains after the stable components have relaxed. Each cell's random spikes disturb its outgoing synaptic activation. The circuit's return flow determines the lasting shift in memory. This calculation uses the weak noise and conditional independence assumptions, with rates and return flow evaluated near one fixed point.

section_list.title: Symmetric weights express diffusion through tuning curves
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** The general formula requires the left vector of the network dynamics. When $W_{ij}=W_{ji}$, can we express it through the tuning curves and neural transfer function? Symmetric connections make each cell affect another cell's input with the same weight that it receives in return, while their firing responses can still differ. We retain the common synaptic time constant, a stable continuous family, and the weak noise and conditional independence assumptions.
