# Boundaries and drift change memory error over long delays {#ch:MEMORY-LONG-DELAYS} [A rate of random spreading measured near one stored value does not yet tell us how memory error behaves after a long wait.]{.key-statement} The value may approach a boundary, wrap around an angular range, or reach a region where the spreading rate differs. A consistent movement of the average value would also change the error without being captured by the rate of random spreading alone. We begin by following the distribution of stored values across repeated trials, using the local diffusion coefficient derived in the preceding chapter. This shows why errors can keep growing on a line but level off when angular error is measured within one turn. We then separate random spreading from systematic drift and make the noise assumptions explicit. Finally, the paper's figures show what its network simulations test and distinguish movement of the memory from uncertainty when another circuit reads it. That second uncertainty motivates the information calculation that follows. Here $\theta$ is the current stored value and $\Theta$ its common initial value across trials. The local diffusion coefficient $D(\theta)$ comes from the weak spike fluctuations derived in the [preceding chapter](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion), after stable disturbances have relaxed. For constant $D$, displacement variance is $2Dt$ before boundaries matter and when there is no systematic drift. ## Long delay errors depend on boundaries and local diffusion {#sec:MEMORY-LONG-TIME} **Neural mechanism.** Spike fluctuations keep shifting the stored value after the cue has ended. The local diffusion coefficient describes the variance of those shifts after stable disturbances have relaxed. It does not by itself say that variance grows at the same rate forever: boundaries and variation of $D$ can change the long time behavior. We first keep $D$ constant, so the line and circle differ only in how the memory coordinate is bounded. **Mathematical derivation.** Let $p(\theta,t)$ be the density of the memory coordinate across repeated trials initialized at $\Theta$. [The [**Itô convention**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} evaluates a state-dependent noise coefficient at the beginning of each increment.]{.definition-explanation} A density equation tracks how small random increments redistribute probability. The calculation below first obtains that equation for a general state-dependent $D$. Constant $D$ then gives the line and circle solutions. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: from random increments to the memory density equation"} To pass from random increments to a density equation, choose any smooth function $F(\theta)$. In a short interval $dt$, the zero-drift Itô increment has conditional mean zero and conditional second moment $2D(\theta)dt$. Taylor expansion at the starting coordinate gives $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[F(\theta+d\theta)-F(\theta)\mid\theta] &=F'(\theta)\mathbb E[d\theta\mid\theta] +\tfrac12F''(\theta)\mathbb E[(d\theta)^2\mid\theta]+o(dt)\\ &=D(\theta)F''(\theta)dt+o(dt). \end{aligned} $$ The higher-order terms vanish faster than $dt$ in this diffusion approximation. Averaging over the starting-coordinate density and dividing by $dt$ gives $$ \frac{d}{dt}\int F(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta =\int F''(\theta)D(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta. $$ Take $F$ to vanish outside an interior region, or use boundaries for which the integration terms vanish. Integrating by parts twice moves both derivatives from $F$ onto the product $Dp$. Because the resulting identity holds for every such smooth $F$, it gives the density equation below. ::: [In the zero-drift diffusion approximation, this density evolves according to the [**Fokker Planck equation**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}:]{.definition-explanation} $$ \frac{\partial p}{\partial t} =\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}[D(\theta)p], \qquad p(\theta,0)=\delta(\theta-\Theta). $$ [Here the [**Dirac delta**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} denotes a point mass: initially all probability is at $\Theta$.]{.definition-explanation} It differs from the earlier zero-or-one symbol $\delta_{ij}$. For constant $D$ on an unbounded line, the Gaussian solution is $$ p(\theta,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}} \exp\left[-\frac{(\theta-\Theta)^2}{4Dt}\right]. $$ Its variance is $2Dt$. For an angular coordinate, add the densities at all displacements $\theta-\Theta+2\pi k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, to wrap the Gaussian around the circle. This wrapped sum appears in [SI Eq. S31, p. 7](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=7&zoom=125,0,483). At long times the density approaches $1/(2\pi)$. If angular errors are reported in $[-\pi,\pi)$, their limiting mean squared value is $$ \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^2dx=\frac{\pi^2}{3}. $$ **Interpretation.** [The flattening of a ring network's error curve can therefore occur while its local noise mechanism remains unchanged. It reflects the bounded way angular error is reported.]{.key-statement}[^p1-fp] For $D=0.5\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}$, the plots show how the density and squared error change with delay.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-LINE-RING}}
As the wrapped density approaches uniform, its mean squared error approaches $\pi^2/3$. The unbounded line error keeps growing. **Neural mechanism.** The rate of random spreading can change as the stored value changes, because the current firing rates set the spike variability. The supplement illustrates this dependence with mutual excitation, $W_{12}=W_{21}=1$, biases $(b_0,-b_0)$, and the same linear transfer rule. The fixed activation states are $(\theta+b_0/2,\theta-b_0/2)$. Now $\mathbf u=(1,1)^T$, $\mathbf v=(1/2,1/2)^T$. Here $\theta$ is an activation coordinate, not an angle, and both steady rates are positive only when $\theta>|b_0|/2$. When both activations rise together, each cell raises the other's firing enough to replace the extra synaptic decay. This common increase persists and changes the stored value. A disturbance in their difference instead decays toward the difference set by the biases. Larger $\theta$ raises both firing rates and hence both Poisson count variances. Because the projection weights stay fixed in this example, more of that variability remains as memory error. **Mathematical derivation.** When $D$ varies with state, the zero drift stochastic equation is $d\theta=\sqrt{2D(\theta)}\,dB$ with the Itô convention. Under conditions that remove boundary terms, the density equation gives $$ \frac{d}{dt}E[\theta]=0, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{Var}(\theta)=2E[D(\theta)]. $$ To obtain these identities, multiply the density equation by $\theta$ or $(\theta-\Theta)^2$, integrate over $\theta$, and integrate by parts twice. The second derivatives of these functions are respectively zero and two, giving the two identities. A similar calculation for the smooth function $D$ gives $dE[D]/dt=E[DD'']$. Expanding at $t=0$ therefore yields $$ \operatorname{Var}(\theta) =2D(\Theta)t+D(\Theta)D''(\Theta)t^2+O(t^3). $$ This is [SI Eq. S37, p. 8](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=8&zoom=125,0,602).[^p1-variable] For the mutual excitation network, substituting $v_1=v_2=1/2$ into the diffusion formula gives $$ 2D=\frac{1}{4}(\bar r_1+\bar r_2)=\frac{\theta}{2\tau}, \qquad D=\frac{\theta}{4\tau}. $$ **Interpretation.** A state dependent $D$ need not produce a nonlinear increase of variance with time. If $D$ is linear in $\theta$, then $E[D(\theta)]=D(E[\theta])=D(\Theta)$, so the variance remains linear while the process stays within the model's valid domain. The implied variance for this network is $\Theta t/(2\tau)$, agreeing with [SI Eq. S41, p. 9](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=9&zoom=125,0,383) and the slope tested in [Fig. S1, p. 10](ch-memory-long-delays.html#fig-paper-memory-s1). SI Eq. S40 instead prints $D=\theta/(2\tau)$. Under the convention used throughout this guide, that displayed value differs by a factor of two from the direct projection and S41.[^p1-excitation]
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure S1
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-S1}}
## A diffusion calculation does not determine systematic drift {#sec:MEMORY-DRIFT-SCOPE} **Neural mechanism.** [Repeated trials can spread apart even if their average stays at the original value. That random spreading differs from a reproducible movement in one direction.]{.key-statement} Both can occur, and the derivation of $D$ alone does not settle the second question. [The paper assumes that the network is tuned to eliminate systematic drift, meaning a nonzero mean velocity along the attractor.]{.definition-explanation} A deterministic mismatch in weights can create such a velocity. In addition, state dependent noise and curved network dynamics can create a small mean motion even if the noise free model has an exact continuous attractor. The supplement explains that deriving the exact mean motion requires the microscopic jump process, beyond the leading variance calculation ([SI “Systematic drift,” pp. 4–5](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=4&zoom=125,0,362)).[^p1-systematic] **Mathematical derivation.** For state dependent $D$, where the coefficient is evaluated affects the process. [The [**Stratonovich convention**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} uses midpoint evaluation in its limiting increments.]{.definition-explanation} With the same written coefficient and zero written drift, it describes a different process from the Itô equation. Converting the Stratonovich equation into Itô form adds a drift $D'/2$. This follows from the conversion term $bb'/2$ with $b=\sqrt{2D}$ and $bb'=D'$. The supplement uses the difference to estimate a possible scale of noise induced drift, not to identify the exact drift of every neural network. With $D$ of order $1/N$, random displacement over $dt$ is of order $\sqrt{dt/N}$, while such a mean displacement is of order $dt/N$. **Interpretation.** The variance calculation captures the leading random term. [Small changes to weights or biases might cancel the mean drift. They cannot remove the random increments by subtracting a known average.]{.key-statement} A known mean drift can in principle be accounted for by a decoder, but any actual implementation must know that drift and respect the domain and boundary conditions. The independence assumption also has a precise scope. Newly generated spike-count fluctuations are conditionally independent given the present state. Shared recurrent fluctuations can still correlate the observed spike trains over time. An extra source of correlated fluctuations would change the projection formula to $2D=\mathbf v^TQ\mathbf v$, where $Q\,dt$ is their increment covariance. A matching calculation of information would need the probabilities of joint spike patterns. The paper discusses such correlated models as future extensions ([Discussion, p. 5, paragraph beginning “Our spiking model”](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=5&zoom=125,0,142)). It does not prove that every correlated spiking model obeys its Poisson formulas.[^p1-correlation] ## Figures distinguish memory motion from readout error and test diffusion {#sec:MEMORY-FIGURES} **Neural mechanism in the figures.** [Figure 1A, p. 2](ch-memory-long-delays.html#fig-paper-memory-1) shows the definition of the memory coordinate. Start at a green point off the attractor and follow the noise free flow to the black point on it. This endpoint defines the instantaneous attractor state. After one noisy interval, repeat that flow. The difference between the two endpoints is the retained memory change. The relevant projection follows the flow, as in the [tilted two variable example](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization). [In Fig. 1B, an [**activity bump**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a localized peak of population firing rates across the neurons' preferred angles.]{.definition-explanation} The figure separates two sources of error: - During storage, the bump's location has moved away from its initial value $\Theta$. - At the later time, an observer has additional uncertainty about the bump's current location because it sees only a finite sample of spikes. The [information calculation](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-fi) measures this second uncertainty and relates it to diffusion. The [readout chapter](ch-memory-readout.html) then follows observation of the moving state.[^p1-fig1]
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure 1
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-1}}
[Figure 2, p. 3](ch-memory-long-delays.html#fig-paper-memory-2) tests the diffusion calculation in two different network designs. Panel A shows a ring with weights determined by differences of preferred angles. This gives rotational symmetry: rotating the activity pattern around the ring leaves its dynamics unchanged in form. In B, compare the firing rate curves and spike marks in the inset before reading the wandering angular trace. The curve describes rates. The marks show individual spikes. The trace shows the represented angle rather than overall activity amplitude. **Interpretation of the simulation tests.** Panels C and D test different parts of the prediction: - Panel C compares simulated mean squared angular displacements with the prediction from the tuning curves and transfer function. The gray exponential case and black sigmoidal, or S-shaped, case have different transfer functions. The dashed bound is a lower limit for the sigmoidal case, not a separate fitted trajectory. A model can lie above its information bound while still agreeing with the derived diffusion formula. - Panel D follows angular error to longer intervals. Its flattening uses angular wrapping, not a disappearance of noise. The expected limiting value with the caption's error convention is $\pi^2/3$. Panels E to G use mutual inhibition rather than a ring. The two rates in F vary in opposite directions. Their difference represents memory. Panel G compares their displacement statistics with the analytic prediction. This second design matters because the projection argument does not require rotational symmetry. These are simulations checking the model calculation. They are not direct measurements of memory noise in an animal.[^p1-fig2]

## Long delay errors depend on boundaries and local diffusion {#sec:MEMORY-LONG-TIME} **Neural mechanism.** Spike fluctuations keep shifting the stored value after the cue has ended. The local diffusion coefficient describes the variance of those shifts after stable disturbances have relaxed. It does not by itself say that variance grows at the same rate forever: boundaries and variation of $D$ can change the long time behavior. We first keep $D$ constant, so the line and circle differ only in how the memory coordinate is bounded. **Mathematical derivation.** Let $p(\theta,t)$ be the density of the memory coordinate across repeated trials initialized at $\Theta$. [The [**Itô convention**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} evaluates a state-dependent noise coefficient at the beginning of each increment.]{.definition-explanation} A density equation tracks how small random increments redistribute probability. The calculation below first obtains that equation for a general state-dependent $D$. Constant $D$ then gives the line and circle solutions. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: from random increments to the memory density equation"} To pass from random increments to a density equation, choose any smooth function $F(\theta)$. In a short interval $dt$, the zero-drift Itô increment has conditional mean zero and conditional second moment $2D(\theta)dt$. Taylor expansion at the starting coordinate gives $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[F(\theta+d\theta)-F(\theta)\mid\theta] &=F'(\theta)\mathbb E[d\theta\mid\theta] +\tfrac12F''(\theta)\mathbb E[(d\theta)^2\mid\theta]+o(dt)\\ &=D(\theta)F''(\theta)dt+o(dt). \end{aligned} $$ The higher-order terms vanish faster than $dt$ in this diffusion approximation. Averaging over the starting-coordinate density and dividing by $dt$ gives $$ \frac{d}{dt}\int F(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta =\int F''(\theta)D(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta. $$ Take $F$ to vanish outside an interior region, or use boundaries for which the integration terms vanish. Integrating by parts twice moves both derivatives from $F$ onto the product $Dp$. Because the resulting identity holds for every such smooth $F$, it gives the density equation below. ::: [In the zero-drift diffusion approximation, this density evolves according to the [**Fokker Planck equation**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}:]{.definition-explanation} $$ \frac{\partial p}{\partial t} =\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}[D(\theta)p], \qquad p(\theta,0)=\delta(\theta-\Theta). $$ [Here the [**Dirac delta**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} denotes a point mass: initially all probability is at $\Theta$.]{.definition-explanation} It differs from the earlier zero-or-one symbol $\delta_{ij}$. For constant $D$ on an unbounded line, the Gaussian solution is $$ p(\theta,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}} \exp\left[-\frac{(\theta-\Theta)^2}{4Dt}\right]. $$ Its variance is $2Dt$. For an angular coordinate, add the densities at all displacements $\theta-\Theta+2\pi k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, to wrap the Gaussian around the circle. This wrapped sum appears in [SI Eq. S31, p. 7](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=7&zoom=125,0,483). At long times the density approaches $1/(2\pi)$. If angular errors are reported in $[-\pi,\pi)$, their limiting mean squared value is $$ \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^2dx=\frac{\pi^2}{3}. $$ **Interpretation.** [The flattening of a ring network's error curve can therefore occur while its local noise mechanism remains unchanged. It reflects the bounded way angular error is reported.]{.key-statement}[^p1-fp] For $D=0.5\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}$, the plots show how the density and squared error change with delay.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-LINE-RING}}
As the wrapped density approaches uniform, its mean squared error approaches $\pi^2/3$. The unbounded line error keeps growing. **Neural mechanism.** The rate of random spreading can change as the stored value changes, because the current firing rates set the spike variability. The supplement illustrates this dependence with mutual excitation, $W_{12}=W_{21}=1$, biases $(b_0,-b_0)$, and the same linear transfer rule. The fixed activation states are $(\theta+b_0/2,\theta-b_0/2)$. Now $\mathbf u=(1,1)^T$, $\mathbf v=(1/2,1/2)^T$. Here $\theta$ is an activation coordinate, not an angle, and both steady rates are positive only when $\theta>|b_0|/2$. When both activations rise together, each cell raises the other's firing enough to replace the extra synaptic decay. This common increase persists and changes the stored value. A disturbance in their difference instead decays toward the difference set by the biases. Larger $\theta$ raises both firing rates and hence both Poisson count variances. Because the projection weights stay fixed in this example, more of that variability remains as memory error. **Mathematical derivation.** When $D$ varies with state, the zero drift stochastic equation is $d\theta=\sqrt{2D(\theta)}\,dB$ with the Itô convention. Under conditions that remove boundary terms, the density equation gives $$ \frac{d}{dt}E[\theta]=0, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{Var}(\theta)=2E[D(\theta)]. $$ To obtain these identities, multiply the density equation by $\theta$ or $(\theta-\Theta)^2$, integrate over $\theta$, and integrate by parts twice. The second derivatives of these functions are respectively zero and two, giving the two identities. A similar calculation for the smooth function $D$ gives $dE[D]/dt=E[DD'']$. Expanding at $t=0$ therefore yields $$ \operatorname{Var}(\theta) =2D(\Theta)t+D(\Theta)D''(\Theta)t^2+O(t^3). $$ This is [SI Eq. S37, p. 8](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=8&zoom=125,0,602).[^p1-variable] For the mutual excitation network, substituting $v_1=v_2=1/2$ into the diffusion formula gives $$ 2D=\frac{1}{4}(\bar r_1+\bar r_2)=\frac{\theta}{2\tau}, \qquad D=\frac{\theta}{4\tau}. $$ **Interpretation.** A state dependent $D$ need not produce a nonlinear increase of variance with time. If $D$ is linear in $\theta$, then $E[D(\theta)]=D(E[\theta])=D(\Theta)$, so the variance remains linear while the process stays within the model's valid domain. The implied variance for this network is $\Theta t/(2\tau)$, agreeing with [SI Eq. S41, p. 9](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=9&zoom=125,0,383) and the slope tested in [Fig. S1, p. 10](ch-memory-long-delays.html#fig-paper-memory-s1). SI Eq. S40 instead prints $D=\theta/(2\tau)$. Under the convention used throughout this guide, that displayed value differs by a factor of two from the direct projection and S41.[^p1-excitation]
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure S1
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-S1}}

review_metadata.title: Boundaries and drift change memory error over long delays
review_metadata.purpose: In the memory-network model, random changes in a stored angle accumulate over time. This chapter extends the local spreading calculation to longer delays, where boundaries, angular wraparound, and systematic drift can change the size of the memory error.

section_list.title: Long delay errors depend on boundaries and local diffusion
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** Spike fluctuations keep shifting the stored value after the cue has ended. The local diffusion coefficient describes the variance of those shifts after stable disturbances have relaxed. It does not by itself say that variance grows at the same rate forever: boundaries and variation of $D$ can change the long time behavior. We first keep $D$ constant, so the line and circle differ only in how the memory coordinate is bounded.

section_list.title: A diffusion calculation does not determine systematic drift
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** Repeated trials can spread apart even if their average stays at the original value. That random spreading differs from a reproducible movement in one direction. Both can occur, and the derivation of $D$ alone does not settle the second question.

section_list.title: Figures distinguish memory motion from readout error and test diffusion
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism in the figures.** [Figure 1A, p. 2](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=2&zoom=125,0,439) shows the definition of the memory coordinate. Start at a green point off the attractor and follow the noise free flow to the black point on it. This endpoint defines the instantaneous attractor state. After one noisy interval, repeat that flow. The difference between the two endpoints is the retained memory change. The relevant projection follows the flow, as in the [tilted two variable example](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization).

# Boundaries and drift change memory error over long delays {#ch:MEMORY-LONG-DELAYS} [A rate of random spreading measured near one stored value does not yet tell us how memory error behaves after a long wait.]{.key-statement} The value may approach a boundary, wrap around an angular range, or reach a region where the spreading rate differs. A consistent movement of the average value would also change the error without being captured by the rate of random spreading alone. We begin by following the distribution of stored values across repeated trials, using the local diffusion coefficient derived in the preceding chapter. This shows why errors can keep growing on a line but level off when angular error is measured within one turn. We then separate random spreading from systematic drift and make the noise assumptions explicit. Finally, the paper's figures show what its network simulations test and distinguish movement of the memory from uncertainty when another circuit reads it. That second uncertainty motivates the information calculation that follows. Here $\theta$ is the current stored value and $\Theta$ its common initial value across trials. The local diffusion coefficient $D(\theta)$ comes from the weak spike fluctuations derived in the [preceding chapter](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion), after stable disturbances have relaxed. For constant $D$, displacement variance is $2Dt$ before boundaries matter and when there is no systematic drift. ## Long delay errors depend on boundaries and local diffusion {#sec:MEMORY-LONG-TIME} **Neural mechanism.** Spike fluctuations keep shifting the stored value after the cue has ended. The local diffusion coefficient describes the variance of those shifts after stable disturbances have relaxed. It does not by itself say that variance grows at the same rate forever: boundaries and variation of $D$ can change the long time behavior. We first keep $D$ constant, so the line and circle differ only in how the memory coordinate is bounded. **Mathematical derivation.** Let $p(\theta,t)$ be the density of the memory coordinate across repeated trials initialized at $\Theta$. [The [**Itô convention**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} evaluates a state-dependent noise coefficient at the beginning of each increment.]{.definition-explanation} A density equation tracks how small random increments redistribute probability. The calculation below first obtains that equation for a general state-dependent $D$. Constant $D$ then gives the line and circle solutions. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: from random increments to the memory density equation"} To pass from random increments to a density equation, choose any smooth function $F(\theta)$. In a short interval $dt$, the zero-drift Itô increment has conditional mean zero and conditional second moment $2D(\theta)dt$. Taylor expansion at the starting coordinate gives $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[F(\theta+d\theta)-F(\theta)\mid\theta] &=F'(\theta)\mathbb E[d\theta\mid\theta] +\tfrac12F''(\theta)\mathbb E[(d\theta)^2\mid\theta]+o(dt)\\ &=D(\theta)F''(\theta)dt+o(dt). \end{aligned} $$ The higher-order terms vanish faster than $dt$ in this diffusion approximation. Averaging over the starting-coordinate density and dividing by $dt$ gives $$ \frac{d}{dt}\int F(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta =\int F''(\theta)D(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta. $$ Take $F$ to vanish outside an interior region, or use boundaries for which the integration terms vanish. Integrating by parts twice moves both derivatives from $F$ onto the product $Dp$. Because the resulting identity holds for every such smooth $F$, it gives the density equation below. ::: [In the zero-drift diffusion approximation, this density evolves according to the [**Fokker Planck equation**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}:]{.definition-explanation} $$ \frac{\partial p}{\partial t} =\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}[D(\theta)p], \qquad p(\theta,0)=\delta(\theta-\Theta). $$ [Here the [**Dirac delta**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} denotes a point mass: initially all probability is at $\Theta$.]{.definition-explanation} It differs from the earlier zero-or-one symbol $\delta_{ij}$. For constant $D$ on an unbounded line, the Gaussian solution is $$ p(\theta,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}} \exp\left[-\frac{(\theta-\Theta)^2}{4Dt}\right]. $$ Its variance is $2Dt$. For an angular coordinate, add the densities at all displacements $\theta-\Theta+2\pi k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, to wrap the Gaussian around the circle. This wrapped sum appears in [SI Eq. S31, p. 7](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=7&zoom=125,0,483). At long times the density approaches $1/(2\pi)$. If angular errors are reported in $[-\pi,\pi)$, their limiting mean squared value is $$ \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^2dx=\frac{\pi^2}{3}. $$ **Interpretation.** [The flattening of a ring network's error curve can therefore occur while its local noise mechanism remains unchanged. It reflects the bounded way angular error is reported.]{.key-statement}[^p1-fp] For $D=0.5\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}$, the plots show how the density and squared error change with delay.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-LINE-RING}}
As the wrapped density approaches uniform, its mean squared error approaches $\pi^2/3$. The unbounded line error keeps growing. **Neural mechanism.** The rate of random spreading can change as the stored value changes, because the current firing rates set the spike variability. The supplement illustrates this dependence with mutual excitation, $W_{12}=W_{21}=1$, biases $(b_0,-b_0)$, and the same linear transfer rule. The fixed activation states are $(\theta+b_0/2,\theta-b_0/2)$. Now $\mathbf u=(1,1)^T$, $\mathbf v=(1/2,1/2)^T$. Here $\theta$ is an activation coordinate, not an angle, and both steady rates are positive only when $\theta>|b_0|/2$. When both activations rise together, each cell raises the other's firing enough to replace the extra synaptic decay. This common increase persists and changes the stored value. A disturbance in their difference instead decays toward the difference set by the biases. Larger $\theta$ raises both firing rates and hence both Poisson count variances. Because the projection weights stay fixed in this example, more of that variability remains as memory error. **Mathematical derivation.** When $D$ varies with state, the zero drift stochastic equation is $d\theta=\sqrt{2D(\theta)}\,dB$ with the Itô convention. Under conditions that remove boundary terms, the density equation gives $$ \frac{d}{dt}E[\theta]=0, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{Var}(\theta)=2E[D(\theta)]. $$ To obtain these identities, multiply the density equation by $\theta$ or $(\theta-\Theta)^2$, integrate over $\theta$, and integrate by parts twice. The second derivatives of these functions are respectively zero and two, giving the two identities. A similar calculation for the smooth function $D$ gives $dE[D]/dt=E[DD'']$. Expanding at $t=0$ therefore yields $$ \operatorname{Var}(\theta) =2D(\Theta)t+D(\Theta)D''(\Theta)t^2+O(t^3). $$ This is [SI Eq. S37, p. 8](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=8&zoom=125,0,602).[^p1-variable] For the mutual excitation network, substituting $v_1=v_2=1/2$ into the diffusion formula gives $$ 2D=\frac{1}{4}(\bar r_1+\bar r_2)=\frac{\theta}{2\tau}, \qquad D=\frac{\theta}{4\tau}. $$ **Interpretation.** A state dependent $D$ need not produce a nonlinear increase of variance with time. If $D$ is linear in $\theta$, then $E[D(\theta)]=D(E[\theta])=D(\Theta)$, so the variance remains linear while the process stays within the model's valid domain. The implied variance for this network is $\Theta t/(2\tau)$, agreeing with [SI Eq. S41, p. 9](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=9&zoom=125,0,383) and the slope tested in [Fig. S1, p. 10](ch-memory-long-delays.html#fig-paper-memory-s1). SI Eq. S40 instead prints $D=\theta/(2\tau)$. Under the convention used throughout this guide, that displayed value differs by a factor of two from the direct projection and S41.[^p1-excitation]
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure S1
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-S1}}
## A diffusion calculation does not determine systematic drift {#sec:MEMORY-DRIFT-SCOPE} **Neural mechanism.** [Repeated trials can spread apart even if their average stays at the original value. That random spreading differs from a reproducible movement in one direction.]{.key-statement} Both can occur, and the derivation of $D$ alone does not settle the second question. [The paper assumes that the network is tuned to eliminate systematic drift, meaning a nonzero mean velocity along the attractor.]{.definition-explanation} A deterministic mismatch in weights can create such a velocity. In addition, state dependent noise and curved network dynamics can create a small mean motion even if the noise free model has an exact continuous attractor. The supplement explains that deriving the exact mean motion requires the microscopic jump process, beyond the leading variance calculation ([SI “Systematic drift,” pp. 4–5](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=4&zoom=125,0,362)).[^p1-systematic] **Mathematical derivation.** For state dependent $D$, where the coefficient is evaluated affects the process. [The [**Stratonovich convention**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} uses midpoint evaluation in its limiting increments.]{.definition-explanation} With the same written coefficient and zero written drift, it describes a different process from the Itô equation. Converting the Stratonovich equation into Itô form adds a drift $D'/2$. This follows from the conversion term $bb'/2$ with $b=\sqrt{2D}$ and $bb'=D'$. The supplement uses the difference to estimate a possible scale of noise induced drift, not to identify the exact drift of every neural network. With $D$ of order $1/N$, random displacement over $dt$ is of order $\sqrt{dt/N}$, while such a mean displacement is of order $dt/N$. **Interpretation.** The variance calculation captures the leading random term. [Small changes to weights or biases might cancel the mean drift. They cannot remove the random increments by subtracting a known average.]{.key-statement} A known mean drift can in principle be accounted for by a decoder, but any actual implementation must know that drift and respect the domain and boundary conditions. The independence assumption also has a precise scope. Newly generated spike-count fluctuations are conditionally independent given the present state. Shared recurrent fluctuations can still correlate the observed spike trains over time. An extra source of correlated fluctuations would change the projection formula to $2D=\mathbf v^TQ\mathbf v$, where $Q\,dt$ is their increment covariance. A matching calculation of information would need the probabilities of joint spike patterns. The paper discusses such correlated models as future extensions ([Discussion, p. 5, paragraph beginning “Our spiking model”](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=5&zoom=125,0,142)). It does not prove that every correlated spiking model obeys its Poisson formulas.[^p1-correlation] ## Figures distinguish memory motion from readout error and test diffusion {#sec:MEMORY-FIGURES} **Neural mechanism in the figures.** [Figure 1A, p. 2](ch-memory-long-delays.html#fig-paper-memory-1) shows the definition of the memory coordinate. Start at a green point off the attractor and follow the noise free flow to the black point on it. This endpoint defines the instantaneous attractor state. After one noisy interval, repeat that flow. The difference between the two endpoints is the retained memory change. The relevant projection follows the flow, as in the [tilted two variable example](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization). [In Fig. 1B, an [**activity bump**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a localized peak of population firing rates across the neurons' preferred angles.]{.definition-explanation} The figure separates two sources of error: - During storage, the bump's location has moved away from its initial value $\Theta$. - At the later time, an observer has additional uncertainty about the bump's current location because it sees only a finite sample of spikes. The [information calculation](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-fi) measures this second uncertainty and relates it to diffusion. The [readout chapter](ch-memory-readout.html) then follows observation of the moving state.[^p1-fig1]
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure 1
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-1}}
[Figure 2, p. 3](ch-memory-long-delays.html#fig-paper-memory-2) tests the diffusion calculation in two different network designs. Panel A shows a ring with weights determined by differences of preferred angles. This gives rotational symmetry: rotating the activity pattern around the ring leaves its dynamics unchanged in form. In B, compare the firing rate curves and spike marks in the inset before reading the wandering angular trace. The curve describes rates. The marks show individual spikes. The trace shows the represented angle rather than overall activity amplitude. **Interpretation of the simulation tests.** Panels C and D test different parts of the prediction: - Panel C compares simulated mean squared angular displacements with the prediction from the tuning curves and transfer function. The gray exponential case and black sigmoidal, or S-shaped, case have different transfer functions. The dashed bound is a lower limit for the sigmoidal case, not a separate fitted trajectory. A model can lie above its information bound while still agreeing with the derived diffusion formula. - Panel D follows angular error to longer intervals. Its flattening uses angular wrapping, not a disappearance of noise. The expected limiting value with the caption's error convention is $\pi^2/3$. Panels E to G use mutual inhibition rather than a ring. The two rates in F vary in opposite directions. Their difference represents memory. Panel G compares their displacement statistics with the analytic prediction. This second design matters because the projection argument does not require rotational symmetry. These are simulations checking the model calculation. They are not direct measurements of memory noise in an animal.[^p1-fig2]
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure 2
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-2}}

## A diffusion calculation does not determine systematic drift {#sec:MEMORY-DRIFT-SCOPE}

**Neural mechanism.** [Repeated trials can spread apart even if their average stays at the original value. That random spreading differs from a reproducible movement in one direction.]{.key-statement} Both can occur, and the derivation of $D$ alone does not settle the second question.

<!-- vale ai-tells.ConsequenceParticiple = NO -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO -->
[The paper assumes that the network is tuned to eliminate systematic drift, meaning a nonzero mean velocity along the attractor.]{.definition-explanation} A deterministic mismatch in weights can create such a velocity. In addition, state dependent noise and curved network dynamics can create a small mean motion even if the noise free model has an exact continuous attractor. The supplement explains that deriving the exact mean motion requires the microscopic jump process, beyond the leading variance calculation ([SI “Systematic drift,” pp. 4–5](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=4&zoom=125,0,362)).[^p1-systematic]
<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.ConsequenceParticiple = YES -->

**Mathematical derivation.** For state dependent $D$, where the coefficient is evaluated affects the process. [The [**Stratonovich convention**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} uses midpoint evaluation in its limiting increments.]{.definition-explanation} With the same written coefficient and zero written drift, it describes a different process from the Itô equation. Converting the Stratonovich equation into Itô form adds a drift $D'/2$. This follows from the conversion term $bb'/2$ with $b=\sqrt{2D}$ and $bb'=D'$. The supplement uses the difference to estimate a possible scale of noise induced drift, not to identify the exact drift of every neural network.

With $D$ of order $1/N$, random displacement over $dt$ is of order $\sqrt{dt/N}$, while such a mean displacement is of order $dt/N$. 

**Interpretation.** The variance calculation captures the leading random term. [Small changes to weights or biases might cancel the mean drift. They cannot remove the random increments by subtracting a known average.]{.key-statement} A known mean drift can in principle be accounted for by a decoder, but any actual implementation must know that drift and respect the domain and boundary conditions.

The independence assumption also has a precise scope. Newly generated spike-count fluctuations are conditionally independent given the present state. Shared recurrent fluctuations can still correlate the observed spike trains over time. An extra source of correlated fluctuations would change the projection formula to $2D=\mathbf v^TQ\mathbf v$, where $Q\,dt$ is their increment covariance. A matching calculation of information would need the probabilities of joint spike patterns. The paper discusses such correlated models as future extensions ([Discussion, p. 5, paragraph beginning “Our spiking model”](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=5&zoom=125,0,142)). It does not prove that every correlated spiking model obeys its Poisson formulas.[^p1-correlation]

# Boundaries and drift change memory error over long delays {#ch:MEMORY-LONG-DELAYS} [A rate of random spreading measured near one stored value does not yet tell us how memory error behaves after a long wait.]{.key-statement} The value may approach a boundary, wrap around an angular range, or reach a region where the spreading rate differs. A consistent movement of the average value would also change the error without being captured by the rate of random spreading alone. We begin by following the distribution of stored values across repeated trials, using the local diffusion coefficient derived in the preceding chapter. This shows why errors can keep growing on a line but level off when angular error is measured within one turn. We then separate random spreading from systematic drift and make the noise assumptions explicit. Finally, the paper's figures show what its network simulations test and distinguish movement of the memory from uncertainty when another circuit reads it. That second uncertainty motivates the information calculation that follows. Here $\theta$ is the current stored value and $\Theta$ its common initial value across trials. The local diffusion coefficient $D(\theta)$ comes from the weak spike fluctuations derived in the [preceding chapter](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion), after stable disturbances have relaxed. For constant $D$, displacement variance is $2Dt$ before boundaries matter and when there is no systematic drift. ## Long delay errors depend on boundaries and local diffusion {#sec:MEMORY-LONG-TIME} **Neural mechanism.** Spike fluctuations keep shifting the stored value after the cue has ended. The local diffusion coefficient describes the variance of those shifts after stable disturbances have relaxed. It does not by itself say that variance grows at the same rate forever: boundaries and variation of $D$ can change the long time behavior. We first keep $D$ constant, so the line and circle differ only in how the memory coordinate is bounded. **Mathematical derivation.** Let $p(\theta,t)$ be the density of the memory coordinate across repeated trials initialized at $\Theta$. [The [**Itô convention**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} evaluates a state-dependent noise coefficient at the beginning of each increment.]{.definition-explanation} A density equation tracks how small random increments redistribute probability. The calculation below first obtains that equation for a general state-dependent $D$. Constant $D$ then gives the line and circle solutions. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: from random increments to the memory density equation"} To pass from random increments to a density equation, choose any smooth function $F(\theta)$. In a short interval $dt$, the zero-drift Itô increment has conditional mean zero and conditional second moment $2D(\theta)dt$. Taylor expansion at the starting coordinate gives $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[F(\theta+d\theta)-F(\theta)\mid\theta] &=F'(\theta)\mathbb E[d\theta\mid\theta] +\tfrac12F''(\theta)\mathbb E[(d\theta)^2\mid\theta]+o(dt)\\ &=D(\theta)F''(\theta)dt+o(dt). \end{aligned} $$ The higher-order terms vanish faster than $dt$ in this diffusion approximation. Averaging over the starting-coordinate density and dividing by $dt$ gives $$ \frac{d}{dt}\int F(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta =\int F''(\theta)D(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta. $$ Take $F$ to vanish outside an interior region, or use boundaries for which the integration terms vanish. Integrating by parts twice moves both derivatives from $F$ onto the product $Dp$. Because the resulting identity holds for every such smooth $F$, it gives the density equation below. ::: [In the zero-drift diffusion approximation, this density evolves according to the [**Fokker Planck equation**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}:]{.definition-explanation} $$ \frac{\partial p}{\partial t} =\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}[D(\theta)p], \qquad p(\theta,0)=\delta(\theta-\Theta). $$ [Here the [**Dirac delta**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} denotes a point mass: initially all probability is at $\Theta$.]{.definition-explanation} It differs from the earlier zero-or-one symbol $\delta_{ij}$. For constant $D$ on an unbounded line, the Gaussian solution is $$ p(\theta,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}} \exp\left[-\frac{(\theta-\Theta)^2}{4Dt}\right]. $$ Its variance is $2Dt$. For an angular coordinate, add the densities at all displacements $\theta-\Theta+2\pi k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, to wrap the Gaussian around the circle. This wrapped sum appears in [SI Eq. S31, p. 7](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=7&zoom=125,0,483). At long times the density approaches $1/(2\pi)$. If angular errors are reported in $[-\pi,\pi)$, their limiting mean squared value is $$ \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^2dx=\frac{\pi^2}{3}. $$ **Interpretation.** [The flattening of a ring network's error curve can therefore occur while its local noise mechanism remains unchanged. It reflects the bounded way angular error is reported.]{.key-statement}[^p1-fp] For $D=0.5\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}$, the plots show how the density and squared error change with delay.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-LINE-RING}}
As the wrapped density approaches uniform, its mean squared error approaches $\pi^2/3$. The unbounded line error keeps growing. **Neural mechanism.** The rate of random spreading can change as the stored value changes, because the current firing rates set the spike variability. The supplement illustrates this dependence with mutual excitation, $W_{12}=W_{21}=1$, biases $(b_0,-b_0)$, and the same linear transfer rule. The fixed activation states are $(\theta+b_0/2,\theta-b_0/2)$. Now $\mathbf u=(1,1)^T$, $\mathbf v=(1/2,1/2)^T$. Here $\theta$ is an activation coordinate, not an angle, and both steady rates are positive only when $\theta>|b_0|/2$. When both activations rise together, each cell raises the other's firing enough to replace the extra synaptic decay. This common increase persists and changes the stored value. A disturbance in their difference instead decays toward the difference set by the biases. Larger $\theta$ raises both firing rates and hence both Poisson count variances. Because the projection weights stay fixed in this example, more of that variability remains as memory error. **Mathematical derivation.** When $D$ varies with state, the zero drift stochastic equation is $d\theta=\sqrt{2D(\theta)}\,dB$ with the Itô convention. Under conditions that remove boundary terms, the density equation gives $$ \frac{d}{dt}E[\theta]=0, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{Var}(\theta)=2E[D(\theta)]. $$ To obtain these identities, multiply the density equation by $\theta$ or $(\theta-\Theta)^2$, integrate over $\theta$, and integrate by parts twice. The second derivatives of these functions are respectively zero and two, giving the two identities. A similar calculation for the smooth function $D$ gives $dE[D]/dt=E[DD'']$. Expanding at $t=0$ therefore yields $$ \operatorname{Var}(\theta) =2D(\Theta)t+D(\Theta)D''(\Theta)t^2+O(t^3). $$ This is [SI Eq. S37, p. 8](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=8&zoom=125,0,602).[^p1-variable] For the mutual excitation network, substituting $v_1=v_2=1/2$ into the diffusion formula gives $$ 2D=\frac{1}{4}(\bar r_1+\bar r_2)=\frac{\theta}{2\tau}, \qquad D=\frac{\theta}{4\tau}. $$ **Interpretation.** A state dependent $D$ need not produce a nonlinear increase of variance with time. If $D$ is linear in $\theta$, then $E[D(\theta)]=D(E[\theta])=D(\Theta)$, so the variance remains linear while the process stays within the model's valid domain. The implied variance for this network is $\Theta t/(2\tau)$, agreeing with [SI Eq. S41, p. 9](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=9&zoom=125,0,383) and the slope tested in [Fig. S1, p. 10](ch-memory-long-delays.html#fig-paper-memory-s1). SI Eq. S40 instead prints $D=\theta/(2\tau)$. Under the convention used throughout this guide, that displayed value differs by a factor of two from the direct projection and S41.[^p1-excitation]
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure S1
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-S1}}

review_metadata.title: Boundaries and drift change memory error over long delays
review_metadata.purpose: In the memory-network model, random changes in a stored angle accumulate over time. This chapter extends the local spreading calculation to longer delays, where boundaries, angular wraparound, and systematic drift can change the size of the memory error.

section_list.title: Long delay errors depend on boundaries and local diffusion
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** Spike fluctuations keep shifting the stored value after the cue has ended. The local diffusion coefficient describes the variance of those shifts after stable disturbances have relaxed. We first keep $D$ constant, so the line and circle differ only in how the memory coordinate is bounded.

section_list.title: A diffusion calculation does not determine systematic drift
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** Repeated trials can spread apart even if their average stays at the original value. That random spreading differs from a reproducible movement in one direction. Both can occur, and the derivation of $D$ alone does not settle the second question.

# Boundaries and drift change memory error over long delays {#ch:MEMORY-LONG-DELAYS} [A rate of random spreading measured near one stored value does not yet tell us how memory error behaves after a long wait.]{.key-statement} The value may approach a boundary, wrap around an angular range, or reach a region where the spreading rate differs. A consistent movement of the average value would also change the error without being captured by the rate of random spreading alone. We begin by following the distribution of stored values across repeated trials, using the local diffusion coefficient derived in the preceding chapter. This shows why errors can keep growing on a line but level off when angular error is measured within one turn. We then separate random spreading from systematic drift and make the noise assumptions explicit. Finally, the paper's figures show what its network simulations test and distinguish movement of the memory from uncertainty when another circuit reads it. That second uncertainty motivates the information calculation that follows. Here $\theta$ is the current stored value and $\Theta$ its common initial value across trials. The local diffusion coefficient $D(\theta)$ comes from the weak spike fluctuations derived in the [preceding chapter](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion), after stable disturbances have relaxed. For constant $D$, displacement variance is $2Dt$ before boundaries matter and when there is no systematic drift. ## Long delay errors depend on boundaries and local diffusion {#sec:MEMORY-LONG-TIME} **Neural mechanism.** Spike fluctuations keep shifting the stored value after the cue has ended. The local diffusion coefficient describes the variance of those shifts after stable disturbances have relaxed. It does not by itself say that variance grows at the same rate forever: boundaries and variation of $D$ can change the long time behavior. We first keep $D$ constant, so the line and circle differ only in how the memory coordinate is bounded. **Mathematical derivation.** Let $p(\theta,t)$ be the density of the memory coordinate across repeated trials initialized at $\Theta$. [The [**Itô convention**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} evaluates a state-dependent noise coefficient at the beginning of each increment.]{.definition-explanation} A density equation tracks how small random increments redistribute probability. The calculation below first obtains that equation for a general state-dependent $D$. Constant $D$ then gives the line and circle solutions. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: from random increments to the memory density equation"} To pass from random increments to a density equation, choose any smooth function $F(\theta)$. In a short interval $dt$, the zero-drift Itô increment has conditional mean zero and conditional second moment $2D(\theta)dt$. Taylor expansion at the starting coordinate gives $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[F(\theta+d\theta)-F(\theta)\mid\theta] &=F'(\theta)\mathbb E[d\theta\mid\theta] +\tfrac12F''(\theta)\mathbb E[(d\theta)^2\mid\theta]+o(dt)\\ &=D(\theta)F''(\theta)dt+o(dt). \end{aligned} $$ The higher-order terms vanish faster than $dt$ in this diffusion approximation. Averaging over the starting-coordinate density and dividing by $dt$ gives $$ \frac{d}{dt}\int F(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta =\int F''(\theta)D(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta. $$ Take $F$ to vanish outside an interior region, or use boundaries for which the integration terms vanish. Integrating by parts twice moves both derivatives from $F$ onto the product $Dp$. Because the resulting identity holds for every such smooth $F$, it gives the density equation below. ::: [In the zero-drift diffusion approximation, this density evolves according to the [**Fokker Planck equation**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}:]{.definition-explanation} $$ \frac{\partial p}{\partial t} =\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}[D(\theta)p], \qquad p(\theta,0)=\delta(\theta-\Theta). $$ [Here the [**Dirac delta**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} denotes a point mass: initially all probability is at $\Theta$.]{.definition-explanation} It differs from the earlier zero-or-one symbol $\delta_{ij}$. For constant $D$ on an unbounded line, the Gaussian solution is $$ p(\theta,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}} \exp\left[-\frac{(\theta-\Theta)^2}{4Dt}\right]. $$ Its variance is $2Dt$. For an angular coordinate, add the densities at all displacements $\theta-\Theta+2\pi k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, to wrap the Gaussian around the circle. This wrapped sum appears in [SI Eq. S31, p. 7](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=7&zoom=125,0,483). At long times the density approaches $1/(2\pi)$. If angular errors are reported in $[-\pi,\pi)$, their limiting mean squared value is $$ \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^2dx=\frac{\pi^2}{3}. $$ **Interpretation.** [The flattening of a ring network's error curve can therefore occur while its local noise mechanism remains unchanged. It reflects the bounded way angular error is reported.]{.key-statement}[^p1-fp] For $D=0.5\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}$, the plots show how the density and squared error change with delay.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-LINE-RING}}
As the wrapped density approaches uniform, its mean squared error approaches $\pi^2/3$. The unbounded line error keeps growing. **Neural mechanism.** The rate of random spreading can change as the stored value changes, because the current firing rates set the spike variability. The supplement illustrates this dependence with mutual excitation, $W_{12}=W_{21}=1$, biases $(b_0,-b_0)$, and the same linear transfer rule. The fixed activation states are $(\theta+b_0/2,\theta-b_0/2)$. Now $\mathbf u=(1,1)^T$, $\mathbf v=(1/2,1/2)^T$. Here $\theta$ is an activation coordinate, not an angle, and both steady rates are positive only when $\theta>|b_0|/2$. When both activations rise together, each cell raises the other's firing enough to replace the extra synaptic decay. This common increase persists and changes the stored value. A disturbance in their difference instead decays toward the difference set by the biases. Larger $\theta$ raises both firing rates and hence both Poisson count variances. Because the projection weights stay fixed in this example, more of that variability remains as memory error. **Mathematical derivation.** When $D$ varies with state, the zero drift stochastic equation is $d\theta=\sqrt{2D(\theta)}\,dB$ with the Itô convention. Under conditions that remove boundary terms, the density equation gives $$ \frac{d}{dt}E[\theta]=0, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{Var}(\theta)=2E[D(\theta)]. $$ To obtain these identities, multiply the density equation by $\theta$ or $(\theta-\Theta)^2$, integrate over $\theta$, and integrate by parts twice. The second derivatives of these functions are respectively zero and two, giving the two identities. A similar calculation for the smooth function $D$ gives $dE[D]/dt=E[DD'']$. Expanding at $t=0$ therefore yields $$ \operatorname{Var}(\theta) =2D(\Theta)t+D(\Theta)D''(\Theta)t^2+O(t^3). $$ This is [SI Eq. S37, p. 8](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=8&zoom=125,0,602).[^p1-variable] For the mutual excitation network, substituting $v_1=v_2=1/2$ into the diffusion formula gives $$ 2D=\frac{1}{4}(\bar r_1+\bar r_2)=\frac{\theta}{2\tau}, \qquad D=\frac{\theta}{4\tau}. $$ **Interpretation.** A state dependent $D$ need not produce a nonlinear increase of variance with time. If $D$ is linear in $\theta$, then $E[D(\theta)]=D(E[\theta])=D(\Theta)$, so the variance remains linear while the process stays within the model's valid domain. The implied variance for this network is $\Theta t/(2\tau)$, agreeing with [SI Eq. S41, p. 9](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=9&zoom=125,0,383) and the slope tested in [Fig. S1, p. 10](ch-memory-long-delays.html#fig-paper-memory-s1). SI Eq. S40 instead prints $D=\theta/(2\tau)$. Under the convention used throughout this guide, that displayed value differs by a factor of two from the direct projection and S41.[^p1-excitation]
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure S1
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-S1}}

That random spreading differs from a reproducible movement in one direction.]{.key-statement} Both can occur, and the derivation of $D$ alone does not settle the second question. [The paper assumes that the network is tuned to eliminate systematic drift, meaning a nonzero mean velocity along the attractor.]{.definition-explanation} A deterministic mismatch in weights can create such a velocity. In addition, state dependent noise and curved network dynamics can create a small mean motion even if the noise free model has an exact continuous attractor. The supplement explains that deriving the exact mean motion requires the microscopic jump process, beyond the leading variance calculation ([SI “Systematic drift,” pp. 4–5](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=4&zoom=125,0,362)).[^p1-systematic] **Mathematical derivation.** For state dependent $D$, where the coefficient is evaluated affects the process. [The [**Stratonovich convention**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} uses midpoint evaluation in its limiting increments.]{.definition-explanation} With the same written coefficient and zero written drift, it describes a different process from the Itô equation. Converting the Stratonovich equation into Itô form adds a drift $D'/2$. This follows from the conversion term $bb'/2$ with $b=\sqrt{2D}$ and $bb'=D'$. The supplement uses the difference to estimate a possible scale of noise induced drift, not to identify the exact drift of every neural network. With $D$ of order $1/N$, random displacement over $dt$ is of order $\sqrt{dt/N}$, while such a mean displacement is of order $dt/N$. **Interpretation.** The variance calculation captures the leading random term. [Collecting more spikes helps distinguish nearby activity patterns, but during collection the pattern itself keeps moving.]{.key-statement} The same variability that limits readout also perturbs the recurrent network. More information can permit better stability without ensuring that a particular circuit achieves it.

review_metadata.title: Spike information limits memory stability
review_metadata.purpose: A neuron receiving spikes from a memory circuit has access to information about the stored value. This chapter sets a bound on estimation error under the model’s assumptions and derives the constraint that spike information places on the circuit’s memory stability.

section_list.title: Rate slopes and spike variability determine local information
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** Suppose two nearby memory values produce almost identical rates. A short spike sample cannot reliably tell them apart. If a small change in memory instead produces a large rate change relative to spike variability, that sample is more useful. We need a quantity that measures this local distinction.

section_list.title: Spike information sets a lower bound on memory diffusion
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** The network has no access to its exact firing rates as noiseless numbers. Its recurrent input is built from the same random spikes that an external observer sees. The lower bound on diffusion follows directly by comparing the state sensitivity of the network with the spike information.

section_list.title: Improving persistence depends on what a comparison holds fixed
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** The inequality compares diffusion and information for the same network. To compare different networks, we must say what stays fixed. Otherwise an apparent benefit of a parameter change may come from changing another property at the same time. The comparisons below control how added neurons, altered firing rates, or slower synaptic decay affect the tuning curves and recurrent input.

blocks.caption: Analytic teaching curves $r_A(\theta)=5+35e^{-\theta^2/(2w^2)}$ and $r_B(\theta)=r_A(\theta)+20$, in spikes per second, with chosen width $w=0.6$ rad. The rates have the same derivative. Their individual Poisson information contributions $(r_i^{\prime})^2/r_i$ vanish at the rate peak, where the slope is zero, and are positive on the flanks. Adding baseline firing raises the count noise without changing the slope, reducing local information. These are illustrative tuning curves, not recorded neurons or a demonstrated attractor network.
blocks.alt: The first plot shows two positive peaked rate curves separated by a constant twenty spikes per second. The second shows their shared derivative, positive to the left, zero at the central peak and negative to the right. The third shows squared slope divided by rate for each curve. Both contributions vanish at the center and rise on the flanks. The higher baseline curve contributes less at every point with nonzero slope.

blocks.caption: Analytic teaching calculation for the chapter’s mutual inhibition example, with $b=200$ activation units and $\tau=0.1$ s. The coordinate $\theta$ is an activation difference. For positive rates $r_{1,2}=(b\pm\theta)/(2\tau)$, $J=2000/(40000-\theta^2)$ while $D=1000$ activation units squared per second. The lower bound $1/(2\tau^2J)$ equals $D$ at $\theta=0$ and falls to 750 at $\theta=100$. Higher local information permits a lower diffusion bound but leaves the actual diffusion unchanged in this model. The plotted range stays inside the positive-rate domain $|\theta|<200$.
blocks.alt: Across memory coordinates from minus one hundred sixty to one hundred sixty activation units, internal information has a minimum of 0.05 at zero and grows toward either side. Actual diffusion is a horizontal line at one thousand. The information lower bound meets it at zero and bends downward, reaching seven hundred fifty at coordinate one hundred. A marked gap separates actual diffusion from the bound there.
