# Spike information limits memory stability {#ch:MEMORY-INFORMATION} A neuron that receives spikes from a memory circuit can use them to estimate the value stored by that circuit. [Collecting more spikes helps distinguish nearby activity patterns, but during collection the pattern itself keeps moving.]{.key-statement} The same variability that limits readout also perturbs the recurrent network. Burak and Fiete connect these two effects by deriving a lower bound on memory diffusion from the information in the spikes.[^p1-info-main] The useful quantity is how clearly a short spike sample distinguishes nearby memory values. Comparing that quantity with the random motion already derived gives a minimum rate of memory spreading. This is a limit for a particular network, so using it to compare different networks also requires keeping track of what changes and what stays fixed. More information can permit better stability without ensuring that a particular circuit achieves it. We retain the memory coordinate $\theta$, initial value $\Theta$, firing rate $\bar r_i(\theta)$, synaptic time constant $\tau$, and diffusion convention $\operatorname{Var}(\Delta\theta)=2D\Delta t$. The [network projection](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization) determines which activity changes remain as changes in the stored value. ## Rate slopes and spike variability determine local information {#sec:MEMORY-FI} **Neural mechanism.** Suppose two nearby memory values produce almost identical rates. A short spike sample cannot reliably tell them apart. If a small change in memory instead produces a large rate change relative to spike variability, that sample is more useful. We need a quantity that measures this local distinction. In a short interval $h$, let $n_i$ be neuron $i$'s count. Treat the memory state as locally constant and use the conditionally independent Poisson approximation from the neural model. The calculation below uses positive rates. **Mathematical derivation.** [A [**likelihood**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the probability of observed data as a function of a proposed parameter value.]{.definition-explanation} For the neural model, $$ p(\mathbf n\mid\theta)=\prod_i \frac{[\bar r_i(\theta)h]^{n_i}e^{-\bar r_i(\theta)h}}{n_i!}. $$ Taking the logarithm turns the product into a sum. With $r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta$, $$ \ell(\theta)=\log p(\mathbf n\mid\theta) =\sum_i\{n_i\log[\bar r_i(\theta)h]-\bar r_i(\theta)h-\log(n_i!)\}, $$ $$ S(\theta)=\frac{d\ell}{d\theta} =\sum_i\frac{r_i'}{\bar r_i}(n_i-\bar r_i h). $$ [The [**score**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $S$ measures how the log likelihood changes when the proposed memory value changes.]{.definition-explanation} Its mean is zero because $E[n_i]=\bar r_i h$. Its mean square is $$ E[S^2] =\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i^2}\operatorname{Var}(n_i) =h\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i}. $$ The cross terms vanish by conditional independence, and Poisson variance supplies $\operatorname{Var}(n_i)=\bar r_i h$. [[**Fisher information**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is this expected squared score. The paper divides it by observation duration and calls the result the [**internal Fisher information rate**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}:]{.definition-explanation} $$ \boxed{J(\theta)=\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i}.} $$ [To understand why inverse information is an error scale, let $\hat\theta(\mathbf n)$ be an estimator whose mean equals $\theta$ locally. Such an estimator is [**unbiased**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} Differentiate $E_\theta[\hat\theta]=\theta$ with respect to $\theta$. Under the usual conditions allowing differentiation through the sum over data, $$ 1=\sum_{\mathbf n}\hat\theta(\mathbf n)\partial_\theta p(\mathbf n\mid\theta) =E[\hat\theta S] =E[(\hat\theta-\theta)S]. $$ The last equality uses $E[S]=0$. Cauchy Schwarz now gives $$ 1\le E[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2]E[S^2], \qquad \boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)\ge\frac{1}{Jh}.} $$ **Interpretation.** [This is the [**Cramér Rao bound**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. It is a local bound for regular unbiased estimation.]{.definition-explanation} It does not guarantee that every finite spike sample admits an estimator attaining it. The paper works in a weak noise, informative sample regime where local likelihoods can be approximated as Gaussian and a suitable estimator can approach the bound. [A [**prior distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} represents knowledge about likely parameter values before observing the spikes.]{.definition-explanation} A strong prior, bias, boundaries, or globally ambiguous tuning changes the estimation problem.[^p1-cr] If the coordinate is an angle in radians, $J$ has units $\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The information in a locally stationary interval of duration $h$ is $Jh$, not $J$.[^p1-fi-source] A vanishing rate requires a suitable limit and regularity of the likelihood. Each cell contributes squared slope divided by its count variance per unit time. High rates with zero slope do not distinguish neighboring values, so they contribute no local information. A sharply changing rate can be informative even if it is smaller than another cell's peak rate. The coordinate here describes the network's present internal state. It need not be a currently visible external stimulus. Sensory Fisher information has the same Poisson formula only when the stimulus dependent tuning curves are the relevant rates. Two positive tuning curves with the same changing part isolate the effect of extra baseline firing.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-TUNING-INFORMATION}}
The rate peak has zero local slope, so it contributes no local information at that point. Extra spikes from a constant baseline increase Poisson variability without making nearby values easier to distinguish. See [Internal Fisher information, Eq. 3, p. 2](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=2). ## Spike information sets a lower bound on memory diffusion {#sec:MEMORY-BOUND} **Neural mechanism.** The network has no access to its exact firing rates as noiseless numbers. Its recurrent input is built from the same random spikes that an external observer sees. The lower bound on diffusion follows directly by comparing the state sensitivity of the network with the spike information. **Mathematical derivation.** Cauchy Schwarz bounds a dot product by the product of the two vector lengths. Here the normalization of the memory projection fixes that dot product, while the two lengths measure diffusion and information. From the [projection and diffusion calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion), $$ 2D=\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i, \qquad u_i=\tau r_i', \qquad \sum_i v_i u_i=1. $$ Define two vectors $a_i=v_i\sqrt{\bar r_i}$ and $b_i=r_i'/\sqrt{\bar r_i}$. Their dot product is $$ \sum_i a_i b_i=\sum_i v_i r_i'=\frac{1}{\tau}. $$ Their squared lengths are $\sum_i a_i^2=2D$ and $\sum_i b_i^2=J$. Cauchy Schwarz therefore gives $$ \left(\frac1\tau\right)^2 \le\left(\sum_i a_i^2\right)\left(\sum_i b_i^2\right)=2DJ, $$ or $$ \boxed{D\ge\frac{1}{2\tau^2J}.} $$ **Interpretation.** This proof uses the general left vector formula, so symmetric weights are unnecessary. It is a shorter teaching reconstruction of the scalar proof in SI Section V. Its assumptions are those used to derive $D$ and $J$. It is not a general statement about all possible noisy memory systems.[^p1-bound-source] The units agree: $\tau^2J$ has units of time per coordinate squared, so its reciprocal has the units of diffusion. [Small internal information forces a large minimum diffusion coefficient. Large information allows small diffusion, but does not guarantee it.]{.key-statement} **Neural mechanism.** [Reaching the bound requires the network's retained response to each cell's spike noise to match that cell's information about memory.]{.key-statement} A cell that adds retained noise without helping distinguish nearby values prevents equality. **Mathematical derivation.** Equality requires the two vectors in the proof to be proportional: $$ v_i=c\frac{r_i'}{\bar r_i} \quad\text{for every contributing cell}, \qquad c=\frac{1}{\tau J}. $$ Cells with zero tuning slope cannot contribute extra projected noise if equality is to hold. In a symmetric network, $v_i$ is proportional to $g_i'$, and $r_i'=\phi'(\bar g_i)g_i'$. At each state, the participating cells therefore need a common value of $\phi'(\bar g_i)/\phi(\bar g_i)$. A sufficient way to satisfy this at all states is to choose that ratio equal to the same constant $k$ throughout the relevant input range. Solving $$ \frac{d}{dg}\log\phi(g)=k $$ gives $\phi(g)=A e^{kg}$. **Interpretation.** This exponential family attains equality for symmetric weights with Poisson noise, under the other model assumptions. It is a sufficient condition, rather than a general necessity: the common ratio may depend on the current memory state.[^p1-equality] ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Check: equality can also hold with a linear transfer rule"} The [mutual-excitation example](ch-memory-long-delays.html#sec-memory-long-time) shows why equality does not require an exponential transfer rule. Set its bias $b_0=0$ and use the linear rule $\phi(g)=g/\tau$ on positive inputs. Its fixed states are $s_1=s_2=\theta>0$, with $\mathbf u=(1,1)^T$ and $\mathbf v=(1/2,1/2)^T$. Both rates are $\theta/\tau$, and both rate derivatives are $1/\tau$. Therefore $$ 2D=\frac{\theta}{2\tau},\qquad J=\frac{2}{\tau\theta},\qquad 2DJ=\frac{1}{\tau^2}. $$ Equality holds throughout this family even though its transfer rule is linear. At each state both cells receive the same input, and the ratio $\phi'/\phi=1/\theta$ changes between states. To conclude that equality forces an exponential rule, we need additional restrictions linking the participating input values across cells and states. Continuous variation of the represented value alone does not supply them. This qualification concerns the source's claim that equality requires an exponential rule. The information–diffusion inequality remains unchanged. :::
**Example: the same diffusion with a looser information bound.** In the two cell mutual inhibition model, use $b=200$ activation units and $\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$. The memory coordinate is an activation difference, not an angle. At $\theta=0$ both rates are $1000\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and their slopes are $\pm5\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ per activation unit. Thus $$ J=\frac{25}{1000}+\frac{25}{1000}=0.05, \qquad D=\frac{b}{2\tau}=1000. $$ Here $J$ has units of inverse activation unit squared per second, and $D$ has activation unit squared per second. The bound is $1/(2\tau^2J)=1000$, so equality holds at this balanced state. At $\theta=100$, the rates become $1500$ and $500\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, while their slopes stay $\pm5$. Now $$ J=\frac{25}{1500}+\frac{25}{500}=\frac1{15}\simeq0.06667, \qquad \frac1{2\tau^2J}=750. $$ The actual diffusion remains $1000$. The inequality is strict because these two unequal rates no longer align the network's projection weights with the information optimal weights. This also shows why equality at a special state does not force the transfer function to be exponential on its whole domain. A constant lower bound attained everywhere and an accidental equality at one state are different claims.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-BOUND-STRICTNESS}}
The gap at $\theta=100$ shows why a lower minimum allowed by the inequality is not a reduction in the network’s actual diffusion. See [Diffusion bound, Eq. 4, p. 3](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=3).
**Neural mechanism.** When a circuit stores several coordinates, a spike can shift more than one of them. Comparing each coordinate separately would miss combinations of shifts. The information and diffusion must therefore describe these shared directions. **Mathematical derivation.** For $m$ memory coordinates the information is a matrix, $$ J_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_i \frac{\partial_{\theta_\alpha}\bar r_i\, \partial_{\theta_\beta}\bar r_i}{\bar r_i}. $$ The matrix calculation assumes that every independent small coordinate change can be distinguished through a change in rates, so $J$ is invertible. The matrix bound $2D\succeq\tau^{-2}J^{-1}$ means that every linear combination of coordinate displacements obeys the corresponding variance lower bound. Here $A\succeq B$ means $\mathbf z^T(A-B)\mathbf z\ge0$ for every real vector $\mathbf z$. To derive it, form $N\times m$ matrices $U_{i\alpha}=u_i^\alpha/\sqrt{\bar r_i}$ and $V_{i\alpha}=v_i^\alpha\sqrt{\bar r_i}$. Then $$ U^TV=I,\qquad U^TU=\tau^2J,\qquad V^TV=2D. $$ ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Check: the residual matrix proves the lower bound"} Set $Q=V-U(U^TU)^{-1}$. Expanding $Q^TQ$ and using $U^TV=I$ gives $$ Q^TQ=V^TV-(U^TU)^{-1} =2D-\tau^{-2}J^{-1}\succeq0. $$ ::: **Interpretation.** The bound controls every combination of stored coordinates, including coupled directions that separate scalar bounds would miss. If $J$ is singular, this ordinary inverse formula cannot be used.[^p1-matrix] ## Improving persistence depends on what a comparison holds fixed {#sec:MEMORY-COMPARISONS} **Neural mechanism.** [The inequality compares diffusion and information for the same network. To compare different networks, we must say what stays fixed.]{.key-statement} Otherwise an apparent benefit of a parameter change may come from changing another property at the same time. The comparisons below control how added neurons, altered firing rates, or slower synaptic decay affect the tuning curves and recurrent input. **Mathematical derivation.** Increasing $N$ while retaining the same distribution of tuning curves and scaling weights as $1/N$ keeps individual inputs and rates fixed. The sums in the symmetric formula scale as $N$ in the numerator and $N^2$ in the denominator. Consequently $D\propto1/N$, while $J\propto N$. This is a controlled density or population replication comparison, not a promise about adding arbitrary neurons. If all tuning rates are multiplied by a factor $a$, their slopes are also multiplied by $a$, so $J\mapsto aJ$. For equality achieving exponential networks, $D\mapsto D/a$ immediately follows. The same scaling follows from the symmetric diffusion formula when the change preserves $g_i'$ up to a common scale and preserves the tuning geometry. For a general fixed nonlinear transfer rule, multiplying rates need not preserve those quantities or even the attractor. The paper's rate comparison is made with the tuning shapes and appropriate network scaling held under control.[^p1-scaling] Changing $\tau$ while holding the rate tuning curves and their input relation fixed gives $D\propto\tau^{-2}$ in the symmetric formula. Maintaining those curves requires retuning the network, because $\bar s=\tau\bar r$. At fixed rates, longer-lasting spike effects give larger mean activations. The activation difference between two nearby stored values also grows in proportion to $\tau$. In this symmetric comparison, one spike's unit activation change therefore produces a smaller displacement of the stored value: the projection weights scale as $1/\tau$. The spike variance per unit time stays fixed, so the retained variance scales as $1/\tau^2$. In contrast, holding activation curves and dimensionless weights fixed in the linear two cell example makes rates scale as $1/\tau$, so $D=b/(2\tau)\propto\tau^{-1}$. **Interpretation.** These two statements concern different controlled comparisons. A larger cellular time constant can improve memory stability while the exponent of its effect depends on what the experiment keeps fixed. **Neural mechanism.** The paper also links tuning width to memory persistence. The reason for its opposite predictions in one and three dimensions can be derived from the number of active cells and their slopes. This derivation is a teaching reconstruction of the tuning width argument cited in the main text, rather than a proof that every tuning family follows one power law.[^p1-width] Assume preferred positions $\mathbf c$ have uniform density $\rho$ in a $d$ dimensional stimulus or memory space. Away from boundaries, let identical tuning curves have fixed peak rate $a$ and a common shape $f$: $$ \bar r_{\mathbf c}(\boldsymbol\theta) =a f[(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w]. $$ The width $w$ is varied while $a$, $\rho$, and the shape $f$ are fixed. **Mathematical derivation.** For one coordinate direction $\alpha$, replace the population sum by an integral and substitute $\mathbf z=(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w$: $$ J_{\alpha\alpha} \simeq\rho\int d^d c\, \frac{a^2w^{-2}(\partial_\alpha f)^2}{af} =\rho a w^{d-2} \int d^d z\,\frac{(\partial_\alpha f)^2}{f}. $$ Two factors determine how information changes with tuning width: - The volume element contributes $w^d$ because broader fields recruit more neurons. - The squared slope contributes $w^{-2}$ because broader curves change more slowly. Each diagonal entry therefore scales as $J_{\alpha\alpha}\propto w^{d-2}$. Now restrict the tuning shape $f$ to depend only on distance from its center. Uniformly distributing those centers makes every coordinate direction equivalent: off-diagonal information terms vanish, and all diagonal entries are equal. For an exponential network that attains the matrix bound, $D_{\alpha\alpha}=1/(2\tau^2J_{\alpha\alpha})\propto w^{2-d}$. **Interpretation.** The resulting comparisons are: - Narrower curves help in $d=1$. - Width has no leading effect in $d=2$. - Broader curves help in $d=3$. [These conclusions change under another resource constraint. Fixing the total population spike rate instead of peak rate makes $a\propto w^{-d}$, giving $J\propto w^{-2}$ in every dimension.]{.key-statement} Sparse coverage, a large baseline rate, finite boundaries, correlated noise, or a width too small for the population integral can also change the comparison. Attaining equality means the network reaches the diffusion lower bound for its information rate and synaptic time constant. Minimizing diffusion still requires deciding how much information the allowed architecture and firing budget can supply. If an external stimulus produces the same tuning curves as the network's input free memory states, the sensory and internal Fisher information are equal. In a symmetric exponential network, maximizing this information then improves sensory estimation and minimizes memory diffusion together. This is why the paper suggests that one circuit could support both sensory estimation and memory storage. The mathematical compatibility does not establish where a particular animal stores a memory, and the equality of tuning curves must be checked rather than inferred from the shared formula.[^p1-colocation] [^p1-info-main]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. review_metadata.title: Readout accuracy depends on how a moving memory is observed
review_metadata.purpose: Reading spikes from a memory circuit takes time, during which its stored value can keep changing. This chapter calculates how much longer observation can help recover the value present at a recall cue, and explains why it cannot recover every earlier random displacement.

section_list.title: Storage loss and readout error add under specific assumptions
section_list.summary: **Neural question and model.** At time $T$, a recall cue arrives. The observer must estimate the original value $\Theta$, but only has access to future spikes. The network has already diffused during storage.

section_list.title: Equal weighting becomes harmful when observation lasts too long
section_list.summary: **Neural question and model.** A decoder designed for a stationary state averages its observations with equal weight. That reduces independent observation noise, but late observations reflect a state that has moved further from $x$.

section_list.title: Accounting for diffusion makes readout improve toward a limit
section_list.summary: **Neural question and model.** An observer that accounts for diffusion can use later observations without confusing them with direct measurements of $x$. Their value is limited by the motion separating them from $x$. This is an ideal inference rule for an observer. The readout calculation does not demonstrate a neural circuit implementing it. Its error can be derived by combining information backward from the end of the observation interval.

section_list.title: Limited access can make observation slower
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** A downstream area may receive only some of the memory network's spikes. That reduces its information without reducing the fluctuations that already move the full memory network.

section_list.title: Time scales and noise laws change the bound and its equality condition
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** The time constant in the inequality comes from the dynamics that carry an activation fluctuation into a lasting memory change. If both synaptic activation and firing rate adjust gradually, which time constant matters?

blocks.caption: Original guide construction of storage and cue state readout, based on Burak and Fiete (2012), Supporting Text, p. 12, Eq. S57. The illustrated path is one possible construction, and the orange estimate concerns the state at the cue rather than the state at the end of observation. With the conditions shown, storage and readout variances add because their cross covariance is zero.
blocks.alt: The stored value starts at Theta at encoding time zero and wanders until the recall cue at T. Its cue value is x. Later spikes, collected through T plus L, give an estimate x hat of that cue state. Storage error is x minus Theta. Readout error is x hat minus x. The estimate is drawn separately from the path endpoint. Under the listed independence, unbiasedness and translation assumptions, total variance is two D T plus readout variance.

Ideal readout approaches a normalized variance of one. Simple averaging reaches $2/\sqrt3$ at $z=\sqrt3$ and then worsens. These curves contain no storage variance $2DT$.

Ideal readout coth z falls toward one. Simple averaging z over three plus one over z reaches its minimum at square root of three, two over square root of three, and then rises. # Readout accuracy depends on how a moving memory is observed {#ch:MEMORY-READOUT} When a recall cue arrives, the stored value has already moved. Later spikes can help estimate the value present at that cue, but they cannot reveal the particular random displacements that occurred before it. Waiting for more spikes also allows the network to move further. [The question is how much observation helps when the value being read keeps changing.]{.key-statement} Separating the error accumulated during storage from the error of reading the cue state makes that question precise. Equal weighting of later observations shows why waiting can become harmful. Allowing for the state's motion then shows how observation can keep helping toward a limit, and how access to only some spikes changes the useful duration. The time constants and noise assumptions also need checking before the resulting limits can be compared with the paper's final error claim. As before, the memory coordinate is $\theta$, its initial value is $\Theta$, and its displacement variance is $2Dt$ for constant diffusion coefficient $D$ without boundaries or systematic drift. The storage delay $T$ ends at the recall cue. The observation interval $L$ begins there. The [spike information rate $J$](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-fi) measures how clearly nearby present states can be distinguished, and $\tau$ is the basic model's common synaptic time constant. ## Storage loss and readout error add under specific assumptions {#sec:MEMORY-READOUT-SETUP} **Neural question and model.** At time $T$, a recall cue arrives. The observer must estimate the original value $\Theta$, but only has access to future spikes. The network has already diffused during storage. To solve the readout problem, the supplement approximates the likelihood from each short bin of duration $h$ as Gaussian. Let $x=\theta(T)$ and index subsequent bins by $k$. The equivalent observation model is $$ \theta_{k+1}=\theta_k+\eta_k, \qquad y_k=\theta_k+\epsilon_k, $$ $$ \operatorname{Var}(\eta_k)=2Dh, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_k)=\frac1{Jh}. $$ The Gaussian increments and observation errors are independent in this approximation. The value $y_k$ summarizes information about the state from that bin's population spikes. It is not an additional directly measured physical coordinate. The continuous limit is a convenient mathematical description of the many spike, weak fluctuation regime. It does not assert that an arbitrarily short physical bin already contains enough spikes for a Gaussian fit. The derivations below are exact within this local Gaussian readout model.[^p1-read-gaussian] **Mathematical derivation.** For an unbounded coordinate with constant $D$ and no drift, let $x=\theta(T)$ and let $\widehat x$ estimate that state from later spikes. Write the storage displacement as $s=x-\Theta$ and the readout error as $e=\widehat x-x$. The total recall error is their sum: $$ \widehat x-\Theta=s+e,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(s+e)=\operatorname{Var}(s)+\operatorname{Var}(e) +2\operatorname{Cov}(s,e). $$ Assume the readout is locally unbiased at every possible $x$ and the future noise is independent of the storage history. Conditional on that history, the readout error then has mean zero. Since $s$ is fixed by the history, $\mathbb E[se]=\mathbb E[s\,\mathbb E(e\mid\text{storage history})]=0$. Both errors have zero mean, so their covariance vanishes. [In this readout model, [**translation invariance**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that shifting the represented value does not change the statistics of the readout error.]{.definition-explanation} Its variance is therefore the same at every $x$. Denote it by $V_{\mathrm{read}}(L)$. Using $\operatorname{Var}(s)=2DT$ gives $$ V_{\mathrm{total}}(T,L)=2DT+V_{\mathrm{read}}(L). $$ **Interpretation.** The two terms describe different sources of error: - $2DT$ comes from storage. - $V_{\mathrm{read}}(L)$ concerns estimation of $\theta(T)$ from spikes after $T$. The supplement derives this decomposition for a locally translation invariant diffusion and readout model. State dependence, boundaries, informative priors, or uncertain initial encoding require corresponding changes.[^p1-read-setup] A timeline separates the displacement accumulated before the cue from the error in estimating the cue state afterward.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-READOUT-TIMELINE}}
## Equal weighting becomes harmful when observation lasts too long {#sec:MEMORY-NAIVE} **Neural question and model.** A decoder designed for a stationary state averages its observations with equal weight. That reduces independent observation noise, but late observations reflect a state that has moved further from $x$. **Mathematical derivation.** Write $\theta(T+t)=x+B_D(t)$, where $B_D$ has Brownian covariance $$ E[B_D(t)B_D(s)]=2D\min(t,s). $$ The covariance arises because the two values share increments up to the earlier time. Their later increments are independent. The continuous average is $$ \hat x_{\mathrm{naive}}=\frac1L\int_0^L y(t)dt. $$ Count noise contributes $1/(JL)$: $n=L/h$ bins, each of variance $1/(Jh)$, give average variance $[n/(Jh)]/n^2=1/(JL)$. The motion contribution is $$ \frac{2D}{L^2}\int_0^L\int_0^L\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds. $$ Split the square into its two equal triangles. On the triangle $0\le s\le t\le L$, the minimum is $s$. Therefore $$ \int_0^L\int_0^L\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds =2\int_0^L\!dt\int_0^t\!s\,ds =\int_0^L t^2dt=\frac{L^3}{3}. $$ Combining the terms gives $$ \boxed{V_{\mathrm{naive}}(L)=\frac{2DL}{3}+\frac1{JL}.} $$ The two contributions have opposite dependence on $L$. Differentiating, $$ \frac{dV_{\mathrm{naive}}}{dL}=\frac{2D}{3}-\frac1{JL^2}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad L_{\mathrm{naive}}^*=\sqrt{\frac3{2DJ}}. $$ At that duration the two error terms are equal, and $$ V_{\mathrm{naive}}^{\min} =\frac2{\sqrt3}\sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}. $$ **Interpretation.** [Waiting longer eventually increases error, even with more spikes available. The problem is their equal weighting for a moving state.]{.key-statement}[^p1-naive] ## Accounting for diffusion makes readout improve toward a limit {#sec:MEMORY-IDEAL} **Neural question and model.** An observer that accounts for diffusion can use later observations without confusing them with direct measurements of $x$. Their value is limited by the motion separating them from $x$. This is an ideal inference rule for an observer. The readout calculation does not demonstrate a neural circuit implementing it. Its error can be derived by combining information backward from the end of the observation interval. **Mathematical derivation.** [The [**precision**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} of a scalar Gaussian estimate is the reciprocal of its variance.]{.definition-explanation} Independent Gaussian measurements of one value add precisions. To verify this, multiply likelihoods proportional to $\exp[-(x-a)^2/(2V_a)]$ and $\exp[-(x-b)^2/(2V_b)]$: the coefficient of $x^2/2$ becomes $1/V_a+1/V_b$. Let $P(L)$ be the precision about the state at the beginning of an interval of length $L$, using all observations in that interval and no informative prior. Suppose we have already compressed the later part into a likelihood about the next bin's state with variance $1/P$. Bringing that likelihood one step backward adds transition variance $q=2Dh$, since the next state equals the earlier state plus an independent Gaussian increment. Its precision about the earlier state is therefore $$ \frac{1}{1/P+q}=\frac{P}{1+2DhP}. $$ The new earliest observation adds precision $Jh$. Thus, up to bin endpoint conventions that disappear as $h\to0$, $$ P(L+h)=Jh+\frac{P(L)}{1+2DhP(L)}. $$ Expand the denominator for small $h$: $$ P(L+h)=P(L)+[J-2DP(L)^2]h+O(h^2). $$ The continuous equation and starting condition are $$ \frac{dP}{dL}=J-2DP^2, \qquad P(0)=0. $$ With no observations, precision starts at zero. The term $J$ adds information from new observations. The term $2DP^2$ reduces that gain because later observations are separated from the cue state by diffusion. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Mathematical solution: hyperbolic functions and finite-time readout error"} [The [**hyperbolic tangent**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is $\tanh z=(e^z-e^{-z})/(e^z+e^{-z})$.]{.definition-explanation} [Its [**inverse hyperbolic tangent**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} on $(-1,1)$ is $\operatorname{artanh}z=\tfrac12\log[(1+z)/(1-z)]$, whose derivative is $1/(1-z^2)$.]{.definition-explanation} Set $a=\sqrt{J/(2D)}$ and $k=\sqrt{2DJ}$. Separating variables gives $$ \int_0^{P/a}\frac{dz}{1-z^2}=kL, \qquad \operatorname{artanh}(P/a)=kL. $$ Taking the inverse function and then the reciprocal yields $$ P(L)=\sqrt{\frac{J}{2D}}\tanh(\sqrt{2DJ}\,L), $$ $$ \boxed{V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L) =\sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}\coth(\sqrt{2DJ}\,L).} $$ [The [**hyperbolic cotangent**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is $\coth z=1/\tanh z$.]{.definition-explanation} This backward precision derivation is a teaching reconstruction equivalent to the Gaussian covariance calculation in SI Eqs. S58–S75. It makes explicit how diffusion limits the value of later observations.[^p1-ideal] For short intervals, $\coth z=1/z+z/3+O(z^3)$, so $$ V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L)=\frac1{JL}+\frac{2DL}{3}+O(L^3). $$ The naive and ideal estimators therefore agree through the displayed terms. ::: For long intervals, $$ V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L)\longrightarrow\sqrt{2D/J}, \qquad L^*=\frac1{\sqrt{2DJ}}. $$ **Interpretation.** The ideal observer keeps improving, but the improvement becomes small. Its variance relative to the limiting variance is: - $1.313$ at $L=L^*$. - $1.037$ at $2L^*$. - $1.005$ at $3L^*$. These are variances, so their ratios are not ratios of standard deviations. Using $2DJ\ge\tau^{-2}$ gives $$ L^*\le\tau, \qquad L_{\mathrm{naive}}^*=\sqrt3L^*\le\sqrt3\tau. $$ [Thus the paper's statement about readout within a cellular time constant concerns a characteristic saturation time under full spike access. It does not mean all benefit ends abruptly at $\tau$.]{.key-statement} The naive observer's best variance is only $2/\sqrt3\simeq1.155$ times the ideal observer's asymptotic variance. Its best standard deviation is about $1.075$ times as large.[^p1-time] ## Limited access can make observation slower {#sec:MEMORY-PARTIAL} **Neural mechanism.** [A downstream area may receive only some of the memory network's spikes. That reduces its information without reducing the fluctuations that already move the full memory network.]{.key-statement} **Mathematical derivation.** If every spike is independently retained with probability $\alpha$, the observed rates and their slopes both scale by $\alpha$. Substitution in the Poisson information formula gives $$ J_{\mathrm{obs}}=\sum_i\frac{(\alpha r_i')^2}{\alpha\bar r_i}=\alpha J. $$ The network diffusion coefficient stays $D$. Hence $$ L_{\mathrm{obs}}^*=\frac1{\sqrt{2D\alpha J}} =\frac{L^*}{\sqrt\alpha}, \qquad V_{\mathrm{ideal,obs}}(\infty)=\sqrt{\frac{2D}{\alpha J}}. $$ **Interpretation.** The same factor $1/\sqrt\alpha$ multiplies the naive optimal interval and its minimum variance. The information bound implies $L_{\mathrm{obs}}^*\le\tau/\sqrt\alpha$, which can exceed $\tau$. A selected subset of neurons has exactly $\alpha J$ only when it carries that fraction of the information. A fraction of neurons or spikes chosen by a biased rule need not do so.[^p1-partial]
**Example: limited spike access changes the useful interval.** Take $\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$, $J=10{,}000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $D=0.005\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}$. These values attain the information bound. Full access gives $L^*=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$ and limiting readout variance $0.001\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. The naive optimum is $0.1732\,\mathrm{s}$ with variance $0.001155\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. If $\alpha=0.1$, then $J_{\mathrm{obs}}=1000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The ideal characteristic interval becomes $0.3162\,\mathrm{s}$ and its limiting variance becomes $0.003162\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. The naive optimum becomes $0.5477\,\mathrm{s}$. A two second storage delay contributes $2DT=0.020\,\mathrm{rad}^2$ in both cases, giving total ideal asymptotic variances $0.021$ and $0.023162\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. Limited access leaves the storage error unchanged but increases the time and uncertainty involved in reading the cue state.
## Time scales and noise laws change the bound and its equality condition {#sec:MEMORY-EXTENSIONS} **Neural mechanism.** The time constant in the inequality comes from the dynamics that carry an activation fluctuation into a lasting memory change. If both synaptic activation and firing rate adjust gradually, which time constant matters? In the basic model, the firing rate changes immediately when the summed input changes. Assume symmetric weights. The extension instead lets $r_i$ approach $\phi(g_i)$ gradually, with time constant $\tau_m$, while synaptic activation still decays with time constant $\tau$: $$ \dot s_i=-s_i/\tau+r_i+\xi_i, \qquad \tau_m\dot r_i=-r_i+\phi(g_i). $$ Here $\xi_i$ is the zero mean noise from variable spike generation, with the same Poisson strength as in the basic model. **Mathematical derivation.** In this symmetric weight extension, the linear state is $(\delta\mathbf s,\delta\mathbf r)$ and its deterministic matrix is $$ A=\begin{pmatrix} -I/\tau&I\\ \operatorname{diag}(\phi')W/\tau_m&-I/\tau_m \end{pmatrix}. $$ The right tangent is $(\tau\mathbf r',\mathbf r')$. Write the left zero vector as $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)$. The second block of $(\mathbf a^T,\mathbf b^T)A=0$ gives $\mathbf b=\tau_m\mathbf a$. The first then gives $W^T\operatorname{diag}(\phi')\mathbf a=\mathbf a/\tau$, so symmetry again permits $\mathbf a\propto\mathbf g'$. Normalizing its dot product with the right tangent yields $$ a_i=\frac{g_i'}{(\tau+\tau_m)\sum_jg_j'r_j'}. $$ Only the $s$ block receives the modeled spike noise, so $2D=\sum_i a_i^2\bar r_i$. The symmetric formula consequently becomes $$ 2D=\frac{\sum_i\bar r_i(g_i')^2} {(\tau+\tau_m)^2[\sum_i g_i'r_i']^2}, \qquad 2D\ge\frac{J^{-1}}{(\tau+\tau_m)^2}. $$ **Interpretation.** The sum of the two time constants replaces $\tau$. When one time constant is much larger, it supplies most of that sum. This result belongs to the two stage model and noise placement just described. The paper does not prove that arbitrary collections of biological time constants can always be added.[^p1-two-times] **Neural question and model.** The equality condition also depends on the noise law. To see why, replace Poisson spike-count fluctuations with independent additive Gaussian noise of constant strength $q>0$: $$ ds_i=F_i(\mathbf s)dt+\sqrt q\,dB_i. $$ **Mathematical derivation.** The short interval observation of the mean rate is now Gaussian with variance $q/h$. Repeating the score calculation gives $J=\sum_i(r_i')^2/q$, while projection gives $2D=q\sum_i v_i^2$. The same Cauchy Schwarz proof yields $2DJ\ge\tau^{-2}$. Equality requires $v_i\propto r_i'$ because all cells have the same noise strength. In a symmetric network $v_i\propto g_i'$, so a linear transfer rule supplies the condition by keeping $\phi'(g)$ constant across participating inputs. **Interpretation.** In the Poisson case, variance grows with rate and an exponential rule is a sufficient way to attain equality. The pointwise projection condition remains the general criterion, including the [linear-family counterexample](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-bound) already derived. The difference between these sufficient classes follows from the noise weighting, not from linearity being universally preferable.[^p1-gaussian] This explicit $q$ formulation is a teaching reconstruction that keeps dimensions and the noise normalization visible. The supplement's Gaussian subsection establishes the change in equality condition. Here the matched noise and likelihood derivation supplies all factors of $q$ and $\tau$ without requiring the reader to infer a normalization from SI Eqs. S94–S95. ## Readout saturates, and one printed error bound needs qualification {#sec:MEMORY-FIG3-AND-CAUTION} Figure 3 isolates readout uncertainty, rescaling variance by $\sqrt{2D/J}$ and duration by $L^*$. In these axes the ideal curve is $\coth z$ and the naive curve is $z/3+1/z$. Both diverge like $1/z$ at short durations because too few spikes are available. The plotted features are: - The ideal solid curve approaches one. - The naive dashed curve reaches $2/\sqrt3$ at $z=\sqrt3$, then rises because its equal weighting gives increasing importance to displaced states. - The dotted vertical line marks that naive optimum. The storage delay contribution $2DT$ is not part of these rescaled curves. Figure S2 repeats the comparison for partial access, showing the rightward and upward shifts when $\alpha=0.1$.[^p1-fig3]
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure 3
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-3}}
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure S2
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-S2}}
{{block:fig:MEMORY-READOUT-CURVES}}
More observation keeps helping the ideal reader, with diminishing benefit, while equal weighting eventually gives too much influence to a state that has moved. One printed inequality deserves special care. Main Eq. 6 says that total error is at least $2D(T+\tau)$. SI Eq. S83 uses a lower bound with readout term $2D\tau/\sqrt\alpha$. But the paper's other derived results imply $$ 2DJ\ge\tau^{-2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad J\ge\frac1{2D\tau^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}\le2D\tau. $$ Thus the ideal asymptotic readout term is at most $2D\tau$, with equality when the information diffusion inequality is saturated. Substituting an upper bound for this term cannot establish the printed universal lower bound on total error. Within the local Gaussian model, the defensible statement is $$ V_{\mathrm{total}}(T,L) \ge2DT+\sqrt{2D/J}, $$ with equality approached as $L\to\infty$ for the ideal observer. At saturation this asymptotic expression becomes $2D(T+\tau)$. For partial access the same issue occurs with the factor $1/\sqrt\alpha$. This is an apparent inconsistency between printed formulas, identified by algebra using the supplied sources. It is not a claim that the authors issued a correction.[^p1-printed] For a concrete strict inequality case, keep $\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$ and $D=0.005\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}$ but set $J=40{,}000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Then $2DJ=400\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ exceeds $\tau^{-2}=100\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. The limiting readout variance is $0.0005\,\mathrm{rad}^2$, whereas $2D\tau=0.001\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. At $T=2\,\mathrm{s}$, the Gaussian ideal total limit is $0.0205\,\mathrm{rad}^2$, below $2D(T+\tau)=0.021\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. These values expose the algebraic problem without assuming the bound is saturated. When a continuous attractor circuit is used to accumulate an incoming signal over time, its stored value represents the integral of that signal. The short useful readout interval does not imply a short lifetime for this accumulated value. A tuned circuit can continue to represent the mean of accumulated inputs while its variance grows. A leak would instead pull its mean toward a particular value. [Diffusion limits the accuracy of the integral and the usefulness of long observation. It does not by itself introduce that restoring pull.]{.key-statement} Applying these predictions to an animal also requires checking its spike statistics, tuning, drift, access to spikes, and other sources of movement noise.[^p1-integrator] [^p1-read-setup]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, p. 12, Eq. S57. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). [^p1-read-gaussian]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, p. 13, Eqs. S58–S63 and the approximation paragraph preceding them. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). [^p1-naive]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, pp. 15–16, Eqs. S76–S81. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The double integral calculation exposes the covariances between different times compressed in the printed derivation. [^p1-ideal]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, pp. 13–15, Eqs. S58–S75. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The supplement identifies the solution with a reverse Kalman filter. Here the equivalent precision recursion supplies a derivation without assuming prior knowledge of that filter. The printed plus sign in S71 does not match its hyperbolic cosine solution S73. The recursion independently gives the final S75 result. [^p1-time]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650, main Eq. 5 and Optimal Observation Time; Supporting Text, Eqs. S75 and S80–S81. ## Storage loss and readout error add under specific assumptions {#sec:MEMORY-READOUT-SETUP} **Neural question and model.** At time $T$, a recall cue arrives. The observer must estimate the original value $\Theta$, but only has access to future spikes. The network has already diffused during storage. To solve the readout problem, the supplement approximates the likelihood from each short bin of duration $h$ as Gaussian. Let $x=\theta(T)$ and index subsequent bins by $k$. The equivalent observation model is $$ \theta_{k+1}=\theta_k+\eta_k, \qquad y_k=\theta_k+\epsilon_k, $$ $$ \operatorname{Var}(\eta_k)=2Dh, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_k)=\frac1{Jh}. $$ The Gaussian increments and observation errors are independent in this approximation. The value $y_k$ summarizes information about the state from that bin's population spikes. It is not an additional directly measured physical coordinate. The continuous limit is a convenient mathematical description of the many spike, weak fluctuation regime. It does not assert that an arbitrarily short physical bin already contains enough spikes for a Gaussian fit. The derivations below are exact within this local Gaussian readout model.[^p1-read-gaussian] **Mathematical derivation.** For an unbounded coordinate with constant $D$ and no drift, let $x=\theta(T)$ and let $\widehat x$ estimate that state from later spikes. Write the storage displacement as $s=x-\Theta$ and the readout error as $e=\widehat x-x$. The total recall error is their sum: $$ \widehat x-\Theta=s+e,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(s+e)=\operatorname{Var}(s)+\operatorname{Var}(e) +2\operatorname{Cov}(s,e). $$ Assume the readout is locally unbiased at every possible $x$ and the future noise is independent of the storage history. Conditional on that history, the readout error then has mean zero. Since $s$ is fixed by the history, $\mathbb E[se]=\mathbb E[s\,\mathbb E(e\mid\text{storage history})]=0$. Both errors have zero mean, so their covariance vanishes. [In this readout model, [**translation invariance**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that shifting the represented value does not change the statistics of the readout error.]{.definition-explanation} Its variance is therefore the same at every $x$. Denote it by $V_{\mathrm{read}}(L)$. Using $\operatorname{Var}(s)=2DT$ gives $$ V_{\mathrm{total}}(T,L)=2DT+V_{\mathrm{read}}(L). $$ **Interpretation.** The two terms describe different sources of error: - $2DT$ comes from storage. - $V_{\mathrm{read}}(L)$ concerns estimation of $\theta(T)$ from spikes after $T$. The supplement derives this decomposition for a locally translation invariant diffusion and readout model. State dependence, boundaries, informative priors, or uncertain initial encoding require corresponding changes.[^p1-read-setup] A timeline separates the displacement accumulated before the cue from the error in estimating the cue state afterward.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-READOUT-TIMELINE}}

review_metadata.title: Readout accuracy depends on how a moving memory is observed
review_metadata.purpose: Reading spikes from a memory circuit takes time, during which its stored value can keep changing. This chapter calculates how much longer observation can help recover the value present at a recall cue, and explains why it cannot recover every earlier random displacement.

section_list.title: Storage loss and readout error add under specific assumptions
section_list.summary: **Neural question and model.** At time $T$, a recall cue arrives. The observer must estimate the original value $\Theta$, but only has access to future spikes. The network has already diffused during storage.

section_list.title: Equal weighting becomes harmful when observation lasts too long
section_list.summary: **Neural question and model.** A decoder designed for a stationary state averages its observations with equal weight. That reduces independent observation noise, but late observations reflect a state that has moved further from $x$.

section_list.title: Accounting for diffusion makes readout improve toward a limit
section_list.summary: **Neural question and model.** An observer that accounts for diffusion can use later observations without confusing them with direct measurements of $x$. Their value is limited by the motion separating them from $x$. This is an ideal inference rule for an observer. The readout calculation does not demonstrate a neural circuit implementing it. Its error can be derived by combining information backward from the end of the observation interval.

section_list.title: Limited access can make observation slower
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** A downstream area may receive only some of the memory network's spikes. That reduces its information without reducing the fluctuations that already move the full memory network.

section_list.title: Time scales and noise laws change the bound and its equality condition
section_list.summary: **Neural mechanism.** The time constant in the inequality comes from the dynamics that carry an activation fluctuation into a lasting memory change. If both synaptic activation and firing rate adjust gradually, which time constant matters?

# Readout accuracy depends on how a moving memory is observed {#ch:MEMORY-READOUT} When a recall cue arrives, the stored value has already moved. Later spikes can help estimate the value present at that cue, but they cannot reveal the particular random displacements that occurred before it. Waiting for more spikes also allows the network to move further. [The question is how much observation helps when the value being read keeps changing.]{.key-statement} Separating the error accumulated during storage from the error of reading the cue state makes that question precise. Equal weighting of later observations shows why waiting can become harmful. Allowing for the state's motion then shows how observation can keep helping toward a limit, and how access to only some spikes changes the useful duration. The time constants and noise assumptions also need checking before the resulting limits can be compared with the paper's final error claim. As before, the memory coordinate is $\theta$, its initial value is $\Theta$, and its displacement variance is $2Dt$ for constant diffusion coefficient $D$ without boundaries or systematic drift. The storage delay $T$ ends at the recall cue. The observation interval $L$ begins there. The [spike information rate $J$](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-fi) measures how clearly nearby present states can be distinguished, and $\tau$ is the basic model's common synaptic time constant. ## Storage loss and readout error add under specific assumptions {#sec:MEMORY-READOUT-SETUP} **Neural question and model.** At time $T$, a recall cue arrives. The observer must estimate the original value $\Theta$, but only has access to future spikes. The network has already diffused during storage. To solve the readout problem, the supplement approximates the likelihood from each short bin of duration $h$ as Gaussian. Let $x=\theta(T)$ and index subsequent bins by $k$. The equivalent observation model is $$ \theta_{k+1}=\theta_k+\eta_k, \qquad y_k=\theta_k+\epsilon_k, $$ $$ \operatorname{Var}(\eta_k)=2Dh, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_k)=\frac1{Jh}. $$ The Gaussian increments and observation errors are independent in this approximation. The value $y_k$ summarizes information about the state from that bin's population spikes. It is not an additional directly measured physical coordinate. The continuous limit is a convenient mathematical description of the many spike, weak fluctuation regime. It does not assert that an arbitrarily short physical bin already contains enough spikes for a Gaussian fit. The derivations below are exact within this local Gaussian readout model.[^p1-read-gaussian] **Mathematical derivation.** For an unbounded coordinate with constant $D$ and no drift, let $x=\theta(T)$ and let $\widehat x$ estimate that state from later spikes. Write the storage displacement as $s=x-\Theta$ and the readout error as $e=\widehat x-x$. The total recall error is their sum: $$ \widehat x-\Theta=s+e,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(s+e)=\operatorname{Var}(s)+\operatorname{Var}(e) +2\operatorname{Cov}(s,e). $$ Assume the readout is locally unbiased at every possible $x$ and the future noise is independent of the storage history. Conditional on that history, the readout error then has mean zero. Since $s$ is fixed by the history, $\mathbb E[se]=\mathbb E[s\,\mathbb E(e\mid\text{storage history})]=0$. Both errors have zero mean, so their covariance vanishes. [In this readout model, [**translation invariance**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that shifting the represented value does not change the statistics of the readout error.]{.definition-explanation} Its variance is therefore the same at every $x$. Denote it by $V_{\mathrm{read}}(L)$. Using $\operatorname{Var}(s)=2DT$ gives $$ V_{\mathrm{total}}(T,L)=2DT+V_{\mathrm{read}}(L). $$ **Interpretation.** The two terms describe different sources of error: - $2DT$ comes from storage. - $V_{\mathrm{read}}(L)$ concerns estimation of $\theta(T)$ from spikes after $T$. The supplement derives this decomposition for a locally translation invariant diffusion and readout model. State dependence, boundaries, informative priors, or uncertain initial encoding require corresponding changes.[^p1-read-setup] A timeline separates the displacement accumulated before the cue from the error in estimating the cue state afterward.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-READOUT-TIMELINE}}
## Equal weighting becomes harmful when observation lasts too long {#sec:MEMORY-NAIVE} **Neural question and model.** A decoder designed for a stationary state averages its observations with equal weight. That reduces independent observation noise, but late observations reflect a state that has moved further from $x$. **Mathematical derivation.** Write $\theta(T+t)=x+B_D(t)$, where $B_D$ has Brownian covariance $$ E[B_D(t)B_D(s)]=2D\min(t,s). $$ The covariance arises because the two values share increments up to the earlier time. Their later increments are independent. The continuous average is $$ \hat x_{\mathrm{naive}}=\frac1L\int_0^L y(t)dt. $$ Count noise contributes $1/(JL)$: $n=L/h$ bins, each of variance $1/(Jh)$, give average variance $[n/(Jh)]/n^2=1/(JL)$. The motion contribution is $$ \frac{2D}{L^2}\int_0^L\int_0^L\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds. $$ Split the square into its two equal triangles. On the triangle $0\le s\le t\le L$, the minimum is $s$. Therefore $$ \int_0^L\int_0^L\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds =2\int_0^L\!dt\int_0^t\!s\,ds =\int_0^L t^2dt=\frac{L^3}{3}. $$ Combining the terms gives $$ \boxed{V_{\mathrm{naive}}(L)=\frac{2DL}{3}+\frac1{JL}.} $$ The two contributions have opposite dependence on $L$. Differentiating, $$ \frac{dV_{\mathrm{naive}}}{dL}=\frac{2D}{3}-\frac1{JL^2}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad L_{\mathrm{naive}}^*=\sqrt{\frac3{2DJ}}. $$ At that duration the two error terms are equal, and $$ V_{\mathrm{naive}}^{\min} =\frac2{\sqrt3}\sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}. $$ **Interpretation.** [Waiting longer eventually increases error, even with more spikes available. The problem is their equal weighting for a moving state.]{.key-statement}[^p1-naive] ## Accounting for diffusion makes readout improve toward a limit {#sec:MEMORY-IDEAL} **Neural question and model.** An observer that accounts for diffusion can use later observations without confusing them with direct measurements of $x$. Their value is limited by the motion separating them from $x$. This is an ideal inference rule for an observer. The readout calculation does not demonstrate a neural circuit implementing it. Its error can be derived by combining information backward from the end of the observation interval. **Mathematical derivation.** [The [**precision**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} of a scalar Gaussian estimate is the reciprocal of its variance.]{.definition-explanation} Independent Gaussian measurements of one value add precisions. To verify this, multiply likelihoods proportional to $\exp[-(x-a)^2/(2V_a)]$ and $\exp[-(x-b)^2/(2V_b)]$: the coefficient of $x^2/2$ becomes $1/V_a+1/V_b$. Let $P(L)$ be the precision about the state at the beginning of an interval of length $L$, using all observations in that interval and no informative prior. Suppose we have already compressed the later part into a likelihood about the next bin's state with variance $1/P$. Bringing that likelihood one step backward adds transition variance $q=2Dh$, since the next state equals the earlier state plus an independent Gaussian increment. Its precision about the earlier state is therefore $$ \frac{1}{1/P+q}=\frac{P}{1+2DhP}. $$ The new earliest observation adds precision $Jh$. Thus, up to bin endpoint conventions that disappear as $h\to0$, $$ P(L+h)=Jh+\frac{P(L)}{1+2DhP(L)}. $$ Expand the denominator for small $h$: $$ P(L+h)=P(L)+[J-2DP(L)^2]h+O(h^2). $$ The continuous equation and starting condition are $$ \frac{dP}{dL}=J-2DP^2, \qquad P(0)=0. $$ With no observations, precision starts at zero. The term $J$ adds information from new observations. The term $2DP^2$ reduces that gain because later observations are separated from the cue state by diffusion. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Mathematical solution: hyperbolic functions and finite-time readout error"} [The [**hyperbolic tangent**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is $\tanh z=(e^z-e^{-z})/(e^z+e^{-z})$.]{.definition-explanation} [Its [**inverse hyperbolic tangent**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} on $(-1,1)$ is $\operatorname{artanh}z=\tfrac12\log[(1+z)/(1-z)]$, whose derivative is $1/(1-z^2)$.]{.definition-explanation} Set $a=\sqrt{J/(2D)}$ and $k=\sqrt{2DJ}$. Separating variables gives $$ \int_0^{P/a}\frac{dz}{1-z^2}=kL, \qquad \operatorname{artanh}(P/a)=kL. $$ Taking the inverse function and then the reciprocal yields $$ P(L)=\sqrt{\frac{J}{2D}}\tanh(\sqrt{2DJ}\,L), $$ $$ \boxed{V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L) =\sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}\coth(\sqrt{2DJ}\,L).} $$ [The [**hyperbolic cotangent**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is $\coth z=1/\tanh z$.]{.definition-explanation} This backward precision derivation is a teaching reconstruction equivalent to the Gaussian covariance calculation in SI Eqs. S58–S75. It makes explicit how diffusion limits the value of later observations.[^p1-ideal] For short intervals, $\coth z=1/z+z/3+O(z^3)$, so $$ V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L)=\frac1{JL}+\frac{2DL}{3}+O(L^3). $$ The naive and ideal estimators therefore agree through the displayed terms. ::: For long intervals, $$ V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L)\longrightarrow\sqrt{2D/J}, \qquad L^*=\frac1{\sqrt{2DJ}}. $$ **Interpretation.** The ideal observer keeps improving, but the improvement becomes small. Its variance relative to the limiting variance is: - $1.313$ at $L=L^*$. - $1.037$ at $2L^*$. - $1.005$ at $3L^*$. These are variances, so their ratios are not ratios of standard deviations. Using $2DJ\ge\tau^{-2}$ gives $$ L^*\le\tau, \qquad L_{\mathrm{naive}}^*=\sqrt3L^*\le\sqrt3\tau. $$ [Thus the paper's statement about readout within a cellular time constant concerns a characteristic saturation time under full spike access. It does not mean all benefit ends abruptly at $\tau$.]{.key-statement} The naive observer's best variance is only $2/\sqrt3\simeq1.155$ times the ideal observer's asymptotic variance. Its best standard deviation is about $1.075$ times as large.[^p1-time] ## Limited access can make observation slower {#sec:MEMORY-PARTIAL} **Neural mechanism.** [A downstream area may receive only some of the memory network's spikes. That reduces its information without reducing the fluctuations that already move the full memory network.]{.key-statement} **Mathematical derivation.** If every spike is independently retained with probability $\alpha$, the observed rates and their slopes both scale by $\alpha$. Substitution in the Poisson information formula gives $$ J_{\mathrm{obs}}=\sum_i\frac{(\alpha r_i')^2}{\alpha\bar r_i}=\alpha J. $$ The network diffusion coefficient stays $D$. Hence $$ L_{\mathrm{obs}}^*=\frac1{\sqrt{2D\alpha J}} =\frac{L^*}{\sqrt\alpha}, \qquad V_{\mathrm{ideal,obs}}(\infty)=\sqrt{\frac{2D}{\alpha J}}. $$ **Interpretation.** The same factor $1/\sqrt\alpha$ multiplies the naive optimal interval and its minimum variance. The information bound implies $L_{\mathrm{obs}}^*\le\tau/\sqrt\alpha$, which can exceed $\tau$. A selected subset of neurons has exactly $\alpha J$ only when it carries that fraction of the information. A fraction of neurons or spikes chosen by a biased rule need not do so.[^p1-partial]
**Example: limited spike access changes the useful interval.** Take $\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$, $J=10{,}000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $D=0.005\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}$. These values attain the information bound. Full access gives $L^*=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$ and limiting readout variance $0.001\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. The naive optimum is $0.1732\,\mathrm{s}$ with variance $0.001155\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. If $\alpha=0.1$, then $J_{\mathrm{obs}}=1000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The ideal characteristic interval becomes $0.3162\,\mathrm{s}$ and its limiting variance becomes $0.003162\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. The naive optimum becomes $0.5477\,\mathrm{s}$. A two second storage delay contributes $2DT=0.020\,\mathrm{rad}^2$ in both cases, giving total ideal asymptotic variances $0.021$ and $0.023162\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. Limited access leaves the storage error unchanged but increases the time and uncertainty involved in reading the cue state.
## Time scales and noise laws change the bound and its equality condition {#sec:MEMORY-EXTENSIONS} **Neural mechanism.** The time constant in the inequality comes from the dynamics that carry an activation fluctuation into a lasting memory change. If both synaptic activation and firing rate adjust gradually, which time constant matters? In the basic model, the firing rate changes immediately when the summed input changes. Assume symmetric weights. The extension instead lets $r_i$ approach $\phi(g_i)$ gradually, with time constant $\tau_m$, while synaptic activation still decays with time constant $\tau$: $$ \dot s_i=-s_i/\tau+r_i+\xi_i, \qquad \tau_m\dot r_i=-r_i+\phi(g_i). $$ Here $\xi_i$ is the zero mean noise from variable spike generation, with the same Poisson strength as in the basic model. **Mathematical derivation.** In this symmetric weight extension, the linear state is $(\delta\mathbf s,\delta\mathbf r)$ and its deterministic matrix is $$ A=\begin{pmatrix} -I/\tau&I\\ \operatorname{diag}(\phi')W/\tau_m&-I/\tau_m \end{pmatrix}. $$ The right tangent is $(\tau\mathbf r',\mathbf r')$. Write the left zero vector as $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)$. The second block of $(\mathbf a^T,\mathbf b^T)A=0$ gives $\mathbf b=\tau_m\mathbf a$. The first then gives $W^T\operatorname{diag}(\phi')\mathbf a=\mathbf a/\tau$, so symmetry again permits $\mathbf a\propto\mathbf g'$. Normalizing its dot product with the right tangent yields $$ a_i=\frac{g_i'}{(\tau+\tau_m)\sum_jg_j'r_j'}. $$ Only the $s$ block receives the modeled spike noise, so $2D=\sum_i a_i^2\bar r_i$. The symmetric formula consequently becomes $$ 2D=\frac{\sum_i\bar r_i(g_i')^2} {(\tau+\tau_m)^2[\sum_i g_i'r_i']^2}, \qquad 2D\ge\frac{J^{-1}}{(\tau+\tau_m)^2}. $$ **Interpretation.** The sum of the two time constants replaces $\tau$. When one time constant is much larger, it supplies most of that sum. This result belongs to the two stage model and noise placement just described. The paper does not prove that arbitrary collections of biological time constants can always be added.[^p1-two-times] **Neural question and model.** The equality condition also depends on the noise law. To see why, replace Poisson spike-count fluctuations with independent additive Gaussian noise of constant strength $q>0$: $$ ds_i=F_i(\mathbf s)dt+\sqrt q\,dB_i. $$ **Mathematical derivation.** The short interval observation of the mean rate is now Gaussian with variance $q/h$. Repeating the score calculation gives $J=\sum_i(r_i')^2/q$, while projection gives $2D=q\sum_i v_i^2$. The same Cauchy Schwarz proof yields $2DJ\ge\tau^{-2}$. Equality requires $v_i\propto r_i'$ because all cells have the same noise strength. In a symmetric network $v_i\propto g_i'$, so a linear transfer rule supplies the condition by keeping $\phi'(g)$ constant across participating inputs. **Interpretation.** In the Poisson case, variance grows with rate and an exponential rule is a sufficient way to attain equality. The pointwise projection condition remains the general criterion, including the [linear-family counterexample](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-bound) already derived. The difference between these sufficient classes follows from the noise weighting, not from linearity being universally preferable.[^p1-gaussian] This explicit $q$ formulation is a teaching reconstruction that keeps dimensions and the noise normalization visible. The supplement's Gaussian subsection establishes the change in equality condition. Here the matched noise and likelihood derivation supplies all factors of $q$ and $\tau$ without requiring the reader to infer a normalization from SI Eqs. S94–S95. ## Readout saturates, and one printed error bound needs qualification {#sec:MEMORY-FIG3-AND-CAUTION} Figure 3 isolates readout uncertainty, rescaling variance by $\sqrt{2D/J}$ and duration by $L^*$. In these axes the ideal curve is $\coth z$ and the naive curve is $z/3+1/z$. Both diverge like $1/z$ at short durations because too few spikes are available. The plotted features are: - The ideal solid curve approaches one. - The naive dashed curve reaches $2/\sqrt3$ at $z=\sqrt3$, then rises because its equal weighting gives increasing importance to displaced states. - The dotted vertical line marks that naive optimum. The storage delay contribution $2DT$ is not part of these rescaled curves. Figure S2 repeats the comparison for partial access, showing the rightward and upward shifts when $\alpha=0.1$.[^p1-fig3]
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure 3
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-3}}
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure S2
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-S2}}
{{block:fig:MEMORY-READOUT-CURVES}}
More observation keeps helping the ideal reader, with diminishing benefit, while equal weighting eventually gives too much influence to a state that has moved. One printed inequality deserves special care. Main Eq. 6 says that total error is at least $2D(T+\tau)$. SI Eq. S83 uses a lower bound with readout term $2D\tau/\sqrt\alpha$. But the paper's other derived results imply $$ 2DJ\ge\tau^{-2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad J\ge\frac1{2D\tau^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}\le2D\tau. $$ Thus the ideal asymptotic readout term is at most $2D\tau$, with equality when the information diffusion inequality is saturated. Substituting an upper bound for this term cannot establish the printed universal lower bound on total error. Within the local Gaussian model, the defensible statement is $$ V_{\mathrm{total}}(T,L) \ge2DT+\sqrt{2D/J}, $$ with equality approached as $L\to\infty$ for the ideal observer. At saturation this asymptotic expression becomes $2D(T+\tau)$. For partial access the same issue occurs with the factor $1/\sqrt\alpha$. This is an apparent inconsistency between printed formulas, identified by algebra using the supplied sources. It is not a claim that the authors issued a correction.[^p1-printed] For a concrete strict inequality case, keep $\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$ and $D=0.005\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}$ but set $J=40{,}000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Then $2DJ=400\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ exceeds $\tau^{-2}=100\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. The limiting readout variance is $0.0005\,\mathrm{rad}^2$, whereas $2D\tau=0.001\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. At $T=2\,\mathrm{s}$, the Gaussian ideal total limit is $0.0205\,\mathrm{rad}^2$, below $2D(T+\tau)=0.021\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. These values expose the algebraic problem without assuming the bound is saturated. When a continuous attractor circuit is used to accumulate an incoming signal over time, its stored value represents the integral of that signal. The short useful readout interval does not imply a short lifetime for this accumulated value. A tuned circuit can continue to represent the mean of accumulated inputs while its variance grows. A leak would instead pull its mean toward a particular value. [Diffusion limits the accuracy of the integral and the usefulness of long observation. It does not by itself introduce that restoring pull.]{.key-statement} Applying these predictions to an animal also requires checking its spike statistics, tuning, drift, access to spikes, and other sources of movement noise.[^p1-integrator] [^p1-read-setup]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, p. 12, Eq. S57. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). [^p1-read-gaussian]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, p. 13, Eqs. S58–S63 and the approximation paragraph preceding them. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). [^p1-naive]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, pp. 15–16, Eqs. S76–S81. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, pp. 13–15, Eqs. S58–S75. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The supplement identifies the solution with a reverse Kalman filter. Here the equivalent precision recursion supplies a derivation without assuming prior knowledge of that filter. The printed plus sign in S71 does not match its hyperbolic cosine solution S73. The recursion independently gives the final S75 result. [^p1-time]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. ## Equal weighting becomes harmful when observation lasts too long {#sec:MEMORY-NAIVE}

**Neural question and model.** A decoder designed for a stationary state averages its observations with equal weight. That reduces independent observation noise, but late observations reflect a state that has moved further from $x$.

**Mathematical derivation.** Write $\theta(T+t)=x+B_D(t)$, where $B_D$ has Brownian covariance

$$
E[B_D(t)B_D(s)]=2D\min(t,s).
$$

The covariance arises because the two values share increments up to the earlier time. Their later increments are independent. The continuous average is

$$
\hat x_{\mathrm{naive}}=\frac1L\int_0^L y(t)dt.
$$

Count noise contributes $1/(JL)$: $n=L/h$ bins, each of variance $1/(Jh)$, give average variance $[n/(Jh)]/n^2=1/(JL)$. The motion contribution is

$$
\frac{2D}{L^2}\int_0^L\int_0^L\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds.
$$

<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO -->
Split the square into its two equal triangles. On the triangle $0\le s\le t\le L$, the minimum is $s$. Therefore
<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->

$$
\int_0^L\int_0^L\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds
=2\int_0^L\!dt\int_0^t\!s\,ds
=\int_0^L t^2dt=\frac{L^3}{3}.
$$

Combining the terms gives

$$
\boxed{V_{\mathrm{naive}}(L)=\frac{2DL}{3}+\frac1{JL}.}
$$

<!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = NO -->
The two contributions have opposite dependence on $L$. Differentiating,
<!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = YES -->

$$
\frac{dV_{\mathrm{naive}}}{dL}=\frac{2D}{3}-\frac1{JL^2}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
L_{\mathrm{naive}}^*=\sqrt{\frac3{2DJ}}.
$$

At that duration the two error terms are equal, and

$$
V_{\mathrm{naive}}^{\min}
=\frac2{\sqrt3}\sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}.
$$

**Interpretation.** [Waiting longer eventually increases error, even with more spikes available. The problem is their equal weighting for a moving state.]{.key-statement}[^p1-naive]

review_metadata.title: Readout accuracy depends on how a moving memory is observed
review_metadata.purpose: Reading spikes from a memory circuit takes time, during which its stored value can keep changing. This chapter calculates how much longer observation can help recover the value present at a recall cue, and explains why it cannot recover every earlier random displacement.
